en: The King said:
O Guru, this lineage of Svāyambhuva has been heard by me in detail;
now tell us of the creation of the other Manus, the progenitors of the universe.

O Brahman, the sages proclaim the births and the glorious deeds of Hari within each *manvantara*; please tell them to us who are listening. O Brahman, [tell us] regarding that *manvantara* in which the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, appeared.
"Indeed, the agent has done, does, or will do [this] in the past, future, or today.
Śrī-Ṛṣi said:
"In this kalpa, six Manus have passed, beginning with Svāyambhuva."
The first [skandha] has been narrated to you, in which the origin of the gods and others is described; there,
for the purpose of instructing Dharma and knowledge, the Blessed Lord became the son of that Manu through his two daughters, Ākūti and Devahūtī.
The deeds previously performed by the Blessed Lord Kapila have been described;
O best of the Kurus, I shall now relate what the Blessed Lord Yajña did. The powerful lord, the husband of Śatarūpā, was detached from the enjoyment of desires.

Having renounced his kingdom for the sake of austerity, he entered the forest with his wife. O descendant of Bharata, performing severe penance while touching the earth with only one foot, he remained at Sunandā for a hundred years and spoke this as follows: BhP 08.01.007/3: Having renounced his kingdom for the sake of austerity, he entered the forest with his wife. BhP 08.01.008/1: At Sunandā, for a hundred years, touching the ground with only one foot, BhP 08.01.008/3: while performing this terrible austerity, he recited this, O descendant of Bharata.
The venerable Manu said:
That by which the universe is perceived, but which the universe does not perceive;
that which remains awake while this [universe] sleeps—this [universe] does not know Him, but He knows it.
This entire universe, whatever moves within the world, has the Self as its abode;
therefore, enjoy it by renouncing it—do not covet the wealth of anyone. He whom the eye beholds yet does not behold, whose eye itself is not impaired.
Take refuge in that god, the abode of all beings, who is Suparṇa;
he for whom there is neither beginning, end, nor middle, neither what is one's own, nor what is beyond, neither the internal nor the external.
Since all these belong to him, he is the universe, and he is the great Truth.

He, whose body is the universe, who is invoked by many, the Lord, the Truth, self-luminous, unborn, and ancient—by his own power, which is not subject to birth and so forth, he maintains this world; yet, having cast that power aside through knowledge, he remains inactive.
Then, in the beginning, the sages performed actions for the sake of the cessation of action.
For a person who exerts effort generally encounters lack of effort;
yet the Lord, the Sovereign, acts, for He is not attached therein.
Having attained His own self, His purpose is fulfilled; those who follow Him do not come to grief.
I take refuge in that Lord, who is free from egoism, wise, devoid of desire for rewards, self-sufficient, and not impelled by anything other than Himself;
who, established in His own path, instructs men and is the source of all dharma.
Śrī Śuka said:
Seeing him thus absorbed in meditation, reciting the *Mantra-upaniṣad*,
the Asuras and Yātudhānas rushed toward him out of hunger to devour him.
Observing them thus intent upon him, Hari, the omnipresent Lord, appeared as the Sacrifice (*Yajña*).

Surrounded by the gods known as the Yāmas, he slew [the demons] and ruled over the celestial realm. Svārociṣa was the second Manu; he was the son of Agni, and Dyumatsena, Suṣeṇa, Rociṣmat, and others were his sons.
In that [Manvantara], Indra was Rocana, and the gods were the Tuṣitas and others;
there were seven sages, exponents of the Veda, beginning with Ūrja and Stambha.
And the wife of the sage Vedaśiras was named Tuṣitā.
From her was born the god renowned as Vibhu. Then eighty-eight thousand sages who were firm in their vows followed the vow of him who had been a celibate since childhood.
The third Manu, named Uttama, was the son of Priyavrata;
O King, his sons were Pavana, Sṛñjaya, Yajña, Hotra, and others. The seven sages were the sons of Vasiṣṭha, beginning with Pramada.
Satyā was born as the auspicious Vedaśrutā, and Indra became Satyajit.
From Dharma and Sūnṛtā, however, the Blessed Puruṣottama was born,
renowned as Satyasena, together with those who are devoted to truth.

Accompanied by Satyajit, he slew the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas who were untruthful in their vows and ill-behaved, as well as the malevolent spirits and their hosts. His fourth elder brother was named Tāmasa Manu.
Pṛthu, Khyāti, Nara, Keta, and others were the ten sons of that [Manu]. In the Tāmasa Manvantara, there were seven sages: Satyaka, Haraya, Vīra, Deva, Triśikha, Īśvara, and Jyotirdhāman.
O King, the sons of Vidhṛti were the gods known as the Vaidhṛtis;
they were lost in time, yet by their own splendor they maintained the Vedas.
There too, the Blessed One was born from Harimedha through his wife Hariṇī.
"By whom was he called 'Hari,' by whom was Gajendra liberated from the crocodile?
King Parīkṣit said:
"O Bādarāyaṇa, we wish to hear this from you."

Just as Hari liberated the lord of elephants who was seized by a crocodile, so too the narration of that deed is highly meritorious, auspicious, conducive to well-being, and auspicious; wherever the Blessed Lord Hari, whose fame is most excellent, is sung of.
Śrī Sūta said:
Thus urged by Parīkṣit, who was seated in the vow of fasting unto death, that son of Bādarāyaṇa,
having joyfully greeted the king, spoke while the brāhmaṇas were listening in the assembly of sages.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, there was a preeminent mountain renowned as Trikūṭa;
it was majestic, ten thousand yojanas in height, and surrounded by the Ocean of Milk.
Extended over that much, the mountain Paryaṅka stands illuminating the ocean, the quarters, and the sky with its three peaks made of silver, iron, and gold;
and it brightens all the intermediate directions with other peaks variegated with gems and minerals.
Amidst various trees, creepers, and shrubs, and the resonant sounds of waterfalls,
his feet were washed on all sides by the waves of the milk-ocean;
and with his emerald-like limbs, he turned the earth dark green.
Its caves were frequented by sporting Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, great serpents, Kinnaras, and Apsarases;
and with the sounds of their musical performances, the mountain seemed to roar in its caves out of envy.
The proud lions roar out of fear of others;
the valley is adorned with throngs of various wild animals,
and the beautiful groves of trees are filled with sweet-voiced birds.

In the valley of that great-souled Lord Varuṇa, there were rivers and lakes with clear waters, sandbanks with pebbles like jewels, and breezes from the water fragrant with the scent of the bathing of celestial women.
The pleasure grove of the celestial women,
named Ṛtuman, was adorned on all sides with divine trees that bore flowers and fruit perpetually,
such as mandāras, pārijātas, pāṭalas, aśokas, and campakas.
With mangoes, *piyāla* trees, jackfruit, mangoes, and *āmrātaka* trees;
with betel nuts, coconuts, dates, and *bījapūraka* fruits;
and with *madhuka*, *śāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *asana*, and *arjuna* trees.

With *ariṣṭa*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, *kiṃśuka*, and *candana* trees; with *picumarda*, *kovidāra*, *sarala*, and *suradāru*; and with *drākṣā*, sugarcane, *rambhā*, *jambu*, *badarī*, *akṣa*, *abhaya*, and *āmala*.
It was surrounded by *bilva*, *kapittha*, *jambīra*, *bhallātaka*, and other trees;
in that place was a vast lake with shimmering golden lotuses,
resplendent with the beauty of water-lilies, blue lotuses, *kahlāra* lilies, and *śatapatra* flowers.
It resounded with the humming of intoxicated bees and the melodious warbling of birds;
it was filled with swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks,
ruddy geese, and cranes, and echoed with the cries of water-fowls, lapwings, and *dātyūha* birds.
The water was stirred by the movement of fish and turtles, its surface covered with the pollen of lotuses, and it was surrounded by *kadamba*, *vetasa*, *nala*, *nīpa*,
and *vañjula* trees, as well as by *kunda*, *kurubaka*, *aśoka*, *śirīṣa*, *kūṭaja*, and *iṅguda* shrubs.
It was adorned with *kubjaka*, golden *yūthī*, *nāga*, *punnāga*, and *jāti* flowers; with *mallikā*, *śatapatra*, *mādhavī*, *jālaka*,
and other such trees growing along the banks that bear fruit in every season.
Once, while that leader of the elephant herd was roaming there, taking refuge in the mountain forests with his female elephants,
he crushed trees with their large thickets, thorns, *kīcaka* bamboos,
and reeds; at the mere scent of him, lions, lordly elephants, tigers, and other predatory beasts, along with rhinoceroses, [fled].
Even the great serpents flee in fear, as do the white and black antelopes, the *sarabhas*, the *camaras*,
the wolves, boars, buffaloes, bears, porcupines, cow-tailed monkeys, hyenas, and apes;
yet, by his grace, other small deer, rabbits, and the like roam about without fear.
Scorched by the heat, surrounded by male elephants and female elephants, followed by young calves dripping with rut,
he caused the mountain to tremble on all sides with his great weight; attended by swarms of bees feeding on his ichor,
his eyes rolling with intoxication, he smelled from afar the breeze from the lake, which was thick with the pollen of lotuses.
Surrounded by his herd, which was tormented by thirst, he then quickly approached the vicinity of that lake.

Having plunged into its pure, nectar-like water, which was dusted with the pollen of golden lotuses and blue lilies, he drank his fill from the water drawn up by his own trunk; bathing himself with the waters, his fatigue vanished.

Sprinkling them with water from his trunk and bathing them like a compassionate householder, that elephant— though intoxicated and wretched due to the illusory power of the goat— did not notice his own distress.
O King, at that moment, a certain powerful crocodile, impelled by fate, seized him by the foot in a rage.
Having thus fallen into calamity by mere chance, that exceedingly powerful elephant strode forth according to his strength.

Then the female elephants cried out in distress as they watched their leader, the lord of the herd, being dragged away with force by that stronger one; the other elephants, though they tried to seize his flanks to rescue him, were unable to do so.

As the two lords of elephants thus fought, dragging each other back and forth, a thousand years passed by, O King; and while their lives still remained, the immortals marveled at that wonderful spectacle. Then, after a long period of time, there occurred a great depletion of the elephant king’s mind, strength, and vital energy.

As he was being dragged through the water and sank down, the entire aquatic creature underwent a transformation. When that lordly elephant thus fell into such peril—helpless like an embodied soul subject to fate—he was unable for a long time to effect his own liberation, and after much reflection, he arrived at this thought: *BhP 08.02.030–031* [The text continues: "Alas, how wretched is my condition! I am being dragged by this beast, who is himself bound by the ropes of destiny. I have no power to free myself from this danger, nor can I even move my limbs. [The text continues: "Obeisances to You, O Lord of the Universe, who are the cause of all causes, the witness of all, and the supreme master of all. You are the one who brings about the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. You are the one who bestows the fruits of all actions upon living beings according to their merit and demerit. You are the one who, out of compassion, assumes various forms to protect the virtuous and punish the wicked. You are the one who, though formless, appears in diverse forms through Your own Māyā. You are the one who, though beyond the reach of speech and mind, is perceived by those whose minds are purified by devotion. You are the one who, though devoid of attributes, possesses all auspicious qualities. You are the one who, though one, appears as many. You are the one who, though unborn, takes birth. You are the one who, though actionless, performs all actions. You are the one who, though without beginning, has no end. You are the one who, though without support, supports all. You are the one who, though without form, possesses all forms. You are the one who, though without senses, perceives everything. You are the one who, though without desire, fulfills all desires. You are the one who, though without fear, removes the fear of all. You are the one who, though without refuge, is the refuge of all. You are the one who, though without a body, dwells within all bodies. You are the one who, though without a name, is named by all. You are the one who, though without a lineage, is the source of all lineages. You are the one who, though without a teacher, is the teacher of all. You are the one who, though without a disciple, is the disciple of none. You are the one who, though without a friend, is the friend of all. You are the one who, though without a foe, is the subduer of all foes. You are the one who, though without a weapon, wields all weapons. You are the one who, though without a chariot, rides in all chariots. You are the one who, though without a vehicle, is the vehicle of all. You are the one who, though without a home, dwells in all homes. You are the one who, though without a dwelling, is the dwelling of all. You are the one who, though without a bed, is the bed of all. You are the one who, though without a seat, is the seat of all. You are the one who, though without a path, is the path of all. You are the one who, though without a goal, is the goal of all. You are the one who, though without a beginning, is the beginning of all. You are the one who, though without an end, is the end of all. You are the one who, though without a middle, is the middle of all. You are the one who, though without a part, is composed of all parts. You are the one who, though without a cause, is the cause of all. You are the one who, though without an effect, is the effect of all. You are the one who, though without a quality, possesses all qualities. You are the one who, though without a modification, is the modification of all. You are the one who, though without a change, undergoes all changes. You are the one who, though without a transformation, is the transformation of all. You are the one who, though without a state, is the state of all. You are the one who, though without a condition, is the condition of all. You are the one who, though without a support, is the support of all. You are the one who, though without a foundation, is the foundation of all. You are the one who, though without a basis, is the basis of all. You are the one who, though without a root, is the root of all. You are the one who, though without a branch, is the branch of all. These kinsmen of mine cannot rescue me while I am in such distress; how much less can these elephants and female elephants? Though I am bound by the snare of the Creator’s crocodile, I shall go to Him who is the supreme refuge.
He is the Lord of anyone, even from the powerful serpent of Death who pursues with fierce speed.
We meditate upon Him from whom Death flees in terror, for He protects the one who has approached Him in fear; we seek refuge in that Fearless One.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having thus resolved with his intellect, he composed his mind within his heart.
He chanted the supreme mantra to be recited, which he had learned in his previous birth.
Śrī Gajendra said:
"Oṃ, obeisances unto that Blessed One from whom this world, consisting of consciousness, has arisen."
We meditate upon the Supreme Lord, the Person who is the primordial seed; I take refuge in that Self-born One who is beyond both this world and the other,
he in whom this universe exists, from whom it arises, by whom it is pervaded,
and who is himself this universe.

May He who is the root of the self, who is higher than the highest, protect me— He who, with unimpaired vision, witnesses both that which is manifested and that which is concealed within His own self by means of His own *māyā*.
When all the worlds, their guardians, and all causes have entirely reached dissolution through time...
There was then a dense and profound darkness, beyond which the all-pervading Lord shines forth;
whose station neither the gods nor the sages know—what living being, then, could possibly go there or even describe it?
May He protect me, He whose sequence of movements is difficult to follow, like that of an actor performing with various disguises.

He whose most auspicious abode even the sages— free from attachment, virtuous, and having become the very self of all beings— wander through the forest to behold, following a stainless vow that transcends worldly norms, He, my friend, is my ultimate refuge.
And He for whom there exists neither birth nor action, nor name or form, nor even quality or defect.

Nevertheless, salutations to that Supreme Lord, the Brahman of infinite power, who by his own *māyā* periodically undergoes those [transformations] for the sake of the dissolution and manifestation of the worlds; salutations to the one who is formless yet possesses manifold forms,
whose deeds are wondrous.
Obeisances to the Supreme Self, the witness who is the lamp of the self; obeisances to Him who is beyond the reach of speech, the mind,
and even the consciousness of the wise who have attained Him through purity and dispassion.
Obeisances to the Lord of liberation, the consciousness of the bliss of nirvāṇa;
obeisances to Him who is peaceful, terrible, and deluded, and who possesses the qualities of nature;
obeisances to the one without distinctions, to the Equanimous One, and to the mass of pure knowledge.
Salutations to You, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the presiding overseer of all, the witness;

salutations to the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), the root of the self, and the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). Salutations to the observer of the qualities of all the senses, the cause of all cognition.
Salutations to You who are expressed through the shadow of the unreal, yet appear as the Real;
salutations, salutations to You, the cause of all, the causeless, the wondrous cause;
salutations to the great ocean of all scriptures and traditions, the ultimate liberation, the supreme refuge.

I offer salutations to Him whose heat of consciousness is veiled by the friction-sticks of the *guṇas*, whose mind flashes with the agitation caused by them, who has abandoned the scriptures through the state of *naiṣkarmya*, and who is self-luminous. I bow to the one who is free from abode, who is liberated, and who possesses great compassion, for the sake of releasing creatures like me from their bonds.
Salutations to You, the Lord, the Great One, who are perceived within the minds of all embodied beings by Your own portion as the inward-looking witness;

salutations to the Blessed One, the embodiment of knowledge and the Supreme Controller, who is difficult to attain for those attached to the self, children, wife, wealth, and kin, yet who is meditated upon in their own hearts by liberated souls free from attachment to the modes of nature.
Those who desire dharma, pleasure, wealth, or liberation worship Him and attain their desired goal;

moreover, may He of abundant compassion grant me my prayers and bestow upon me an imperishable body that brings about liberation. For those who have truly taken refuge in the Blessed One, being exclusively devoted to Him, do not desire any object whatsoever.
Singing His most wonderful and auspicious deeds, immersed in an ocean of bliss,
I praise Him— the imperishable Brahman, the Supreme Lord, unmanifest, attainable through spiritual yoga,
beyond the senses, subtle as it were, exceedingly remote, infinite, primordial, and perfectly complete.

He from whom Brahmā and the other gods, the Vedas, and the worlds of moving and non-moving beings are fashioned through the differentiation of names and forms by means of His insignificant portion (kalā);
just as rays issue forth from fire and repeatedly return to the sun, which possesses its own radiance.

Thus, from whom this flow of the *guṇas* proceeds—the intellect, the mind, the senses, and the creation of bodies—he indeed is neither god, nor asura, nor mortal, nor animal; he is neither female, nor neuter, nor male, nor a living being.
He is neither the *guṇa*, nor action, nor existent, nor non-existent; may he, who remains beyond all negation, be victorious in his entirety.
I have no desire to live here or in the hereafter, for I am enclosed within and without by these two wombs.
I desire liberation from that covering of the world of the Self, which is not destroyed by time.
Such as I am, I seek refuge in the creator of the universe, who is both the universe and beyond it, the knower of all things.
I bow down to the Soul of the universe, the unborn Brahman, the supreme state;
I bow down to that Lord of Yoga whom the yogis perceive within their hearts, which have been purified by yoga, once their karma has been burnt away by yoga.

Obeisances, obeisances unto You, whose impetus is irresistible, who possess the three potencies and all the qualities of the intellect; unto the protector of those who have sought refuge, whose power is boundless, and whose path is unattainable by those with wretched senses.
He does not know his own self because he is struck down by the egoistic intelligence produced by Your power.
"I have come here from that Blessed One, whose majesty is difficult to surpass.
Śrī Śuka said:
"Thus, having described Gajendra as being without distinction [from the Lord]..."
When Brahmā and the others, who possessed the conceit of various distinct forms,
did not approach him because he is the soul of all,
Hari, who embodies all the immortals, appeared there.
Perceiving him thus distressed, the Abode of the World,
while being praised by the gods who were chanting hymns along with him, was borne aloft by Garuḍa, who is composed of the Vedic meters.
The wielder of the discus-weapon quickly approached the place where the lordly elephant was; seized by his great strength within the lake,
the distressed elephant saw Hari in the sky with Garuda and the uplifted discus.
Lifting up his hand which held a lotus, he spoke these words with great difficulty:
"O Nārāyaṇa, teacher of all, Blessed One, salutations unto You!
Seeing him thus afflicted, the Unborn Lord suddenly descended.

Out of compassion, Hari quickly rescued from the water the lordly elephant who had been seized by a crocodile; while the eminent sages looked on, he released the elephant from the jaws of the crocodile that had torn open its mouth.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then the celestial sages, Gandharvas, and others, led by Brahmā and Īśāna,
showered down a rain of flowers while praising that deed of Hari.
Divine kettledrums resounded, Gandharvas danced and sang,
and the ṛṣis, Cāraṇas, and Siddhas praised the Supreme Person. That crocodile, assuming a most wonderful form, suddenly appeared.
Released from the curse of Devala, Hūhū, the best of the Gandharvas,
bowed his head to the Lord, the immutable one of excellent renown, and sang praises of that abode of glory whose virtues are worthy of being celebrated.
Compassionately regarded by the Lord, he circumambulated and bowed down to Him;
while the world looked on, he returned to his own world, freed from all sin.
The lordly elephant, through the touch of the Blessed One, was liberated from the bondage of ignorance.
He beheld the form of the Blessed One, clad in yellow garments and possessing four arms.
Indeed, he had previously been King Pāṇḍya, the best of the Draviḍas,
renowned as Indradyumna, who was solely devoted to the vow of Viṣṇu.

Once, at the time of worship, that self-possessed ascetic, wearing matted hair and observing a vow of silence, bathed and worshipped Lord Hari, the Imperishable, in his hermitage on the Kulācala mountain. At that time,
the highly illustrious sage Śukadeva arrived there by chance, surrounded by a multitude of disciples.
Seeing him sitting in secret, having remained silent and failed to offer the customary honors, the sage became enraged.

He pronounced this curse upon him: "This wicked, evil-minded, and undisciplined man, who today has shown contempt for a brahmin, shall enter into darkness—just like that very same elephant of rigid intellect."
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having thus pronounced the curse, the venerable Agastya departed with his followers;
and the royal sage Indradyumna, reflecting upon that which was ordained by fate, remained there.
Having entered the womb of an elephant, which destroys one's memory of the Self, he—
by the power of his worship of Hari— retained his recollection even while in the state of an elephant.
Thus did the lotus-navelled Lord liberate the leader of the elephant herd.
Accompanied by him who had also attained the state of an attendant,
and being praised with songs by Gandharvas, Siddhas, and gods,
He whose vehicle is Garuḍa went to His own abode, performing wondrous deeds.
O Great King, O Best of the Kurus, I have thus related to you this majesty of Kṛṣṇa— the liberation of the lordly elephant—
which leads to heaven, brings fame, removes the impurities of the Kali age, and destroys bad dreams for those who hear it;
and just as the twice-born, desiring their own welfare, recite this very account.

O best of the Kurus, having risen early in the morning, those pure ones recited this for the pacification of bad dreams and other evils; then Hari, the all-pervading Lord who comprises all beings, being pleased, spoke thus to Gajendra while all creatures were listening.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Those who [have seen] me, you, and this lake, as well as the mountain caves, forests,
thickets of cane, bamboo, and reeds, and the celestial trees— "
These peaks are the abodes of me, Brahmā, and of Śiva;
the Ocean of Milk is my beloved abode, as is the radiant Śvetadvīpa.
The Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the mace Kaumodakī are mine.
Sudarśana, Pāñcajanya, Suparṇa the lord of birds,
Śeṣa who is a subtle portion of Me, the goddess Śrī who has Me as her refuge,
Brahmā, the sage Nārada, Bhava, and Prahlāda as well.
The deeds performed by me through my incarnations as the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and others, which yield infinite merit; the Sun, the Moon, and Fire;
the Praṇava, Truth, and the Unmanifest; the cows, the Brahmins, and the Imperishable Dharma.
He also [created] the daughters of Dakṣa as the lawful wives of Soma and Kaśyapa;
Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Nandā, Kālindī, and Sitavāraṇa;
Dhruva; the seven Brahmanical ṛṣis; and the men of virtuous renown.
Those who, having risen at the end of the final watch of the night, being purified and well-composed,
remember my forms, are liberated from all sin;
O dear one, those who praise me with this hymn upon awakening at the close of the night.
"And at the time of their death, I grant them a vast destination.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus instructed him, Hṛṣīkeśa blew his excellent conch shell.
Gladdening the host of the gods, he mounted the king of birds.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, this deed of Hari, which destroys all sins, has been narrated to you.
The meritorious account of the liberation of Gajendra is concluded; now hear about the Raivata Manvantara.
The fifth Manu was named Raivata, the uterine brother of Tāmasa. Bali, Vindhya, and others were his sons, headed by Hārjuna.
O King, Vibhu, Indra, the hosts of gods, Bhūtaraya and others were his sons;
Hiraṇyaroman, Vedaśiras, Ūrdhvabāhu, and others were his twice-born [offspring];
and Vikuṇṭhā was the wife of Śubhra, who had Vaikuṇṭha as his foremost among the gods.
By means of his own portion, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha himself was born from those two;
by him, the world known as Vaikuṇṭha was fashioned, which is honored by all the worlds,
at the request of the goddess Ramā and out of a desire to do what was pleasing to her.
His power and his most exalted qualities have been described;
he who would recount the virtues of Viṣṇu would have to measure the particles of dust upon the earth.
And the sixth Manu was indeed Cākṣuṣa by name, the son of Cakṣus.
Puru, Pūruṣa, Sudyumna, and others were the sons of Cākṣuṣa. Therein, Indra was Mantradruma; the groups of gods were headed by Āpya;
and the sages there, O King, were Haviṣmat, Vīraka, and others.
There too, from Devasambhūti, there was born a son of Vairāja named Ajita,
the Lord and Master of the world,
who by his partial incarnation (aṃśena) churned the ocean and secured the nectar for the gods.
Whirling in the waters, Mount Mandara was supported by the Lord in the form of a tortoise.
King Parīkṣit said: "O brāhmaṇa, how was the ocean of milk churned by the Blessed One?"
For what purpose, and from where, did he support the mountain by assuming the form of an aquatic creature;
how the nectar was obtained by the gods, and what else occurred thereafter—
tell me this most wonderful deed of the Blessed One.
"My mind, long tormented by suffering, finds no satiety in the majesty of the Lord of the Sātvatas as it is being narrated by you.
Śrī Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, having been thus questioned, the venerable son of Dvaipāyana,
after praising the heroic power of Hari, proceeded to describe it.
Śrī Śuka said:
When, in battle, the gods were being struck down by the asuras with sharp weapons and fell in great numbers, their life-breaths departed and they did not rise again;
and when, O King, the three worlds including Indra were [afflicted] by the curse of Durvāsas—
There, deprived of their splendor, rituals such as sacrifices and other rites ceased to be effective.
Having observed this, the hosts of gods, led by Mahendra and Varuṇa,
deliberated among themselves with mantras, yet they could not reach a certain conclusion.
Then they all went to the assembly hall of Brahmā on the summit of Mount Meru.
Bowing down, they reported everything to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
He, beholding Indra, Vāyu, and the others, saw them devoid of strength and shorn of their splendor.

The all-pervading Lord, with a concentrated mind, meditated upon the Supreme Person; then, his face blossoming with joy, that supreme Blessed One spoke to the gods regarding the worlds, which were mostly inauspicious and inhabited by asuras.
I, Śiva, you, as well as the Asuras and others, and the species born of humans, animals, trees, and insects—
all of whom have been sent forth from the portions and parts of His incarnations— we all go for refuge to that Imperishable One,
for whom there is no one to be slain, none to be protected, and no category of those to be neglected or those to be favored.
Nevertheless, for the sake of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he assumes the qualities of passion (*rajas*), goodness (*sattva*), and ignorance (*tamas*) at the proper time.
And now is the moment for his maintenance and protection, as he partakes in goodness (*sattva*) for the welfare of embodied beings.
Therefore, let us go for refuge to the Teacher of the World; he, who is dear to the gods, will grant us peace.
Śrī Śuka said:
O subduer of enemies, having thus addressed the gods along with the creators,
Brahmā went directly to the abode of the Unconquered One, which lies beyond the darkness.
There, with his senses composed, the Lord (Brahmā) offered praise with divine words to Him whose true form had never been seen before, though He had been heard of previously. Śrī Brahmā said:

We bow down to the best of gods, the most excellent one—unchanging, true, infinite, primordial, dwelling in the secret cave of the heart, partless, and beyond the reach of logic; who is reached by the foremost of the mind, yet unexpressed by speech;
the wise one, who is the light of the objects and senses for the self of vital breath, mind, and intellect, and who is sleepless and without blemish.
We go to that imperishable void, the one who appears in the three ages, where there is neither shadow nor light, and where even the wings of vultures do not reach.

I take refuge in that which they call the axle—the wheel of the Unborn, impelled by the Unconquerable One, consisting of mind, with fifteen spokes, three naves, swift as lightning, and eight rims; I take refuge in that Immortal.

That which is of a single color, beyond darkness, the lightless, unmanifest, and boundless—He made this [world] His seat; the wise, by means of the chariot of yoga, worship Him as the Supreme Bird (Upasuparṇa).
No one at all can transcend His Māyā, by which people are deluded and do not know the true meaning.

We bow down to that Supreme Lord who moves equally among all beings, having conquered the self and its qualities. We, who have been created by Him through His own dear body of pure goodness (*sattva*), perceive Him both externally and internally;
yet even the seers do not know His subtle course—how much less the asuras and others, who are dominated by the opposite nature?
He whose feet are this earth, wherein the fourfold creation of beings exists by His own act—
may that Great Person, the self-dependent one of vast opulence, the Supreme Brahman, be gracious. From His seed,
which is water of noble potency, all things are perfected, live, and grow.
May He of great opulence, from whom the worlds and all the guardians of the worlds arise, be gracious unto us;
He whose mind they declare to be Soma, who is the strength, the food, and the life-span of the inhabitants of heaven;
the Lord of mountains and the progenitor of living beings—may He of great opulence be gracious unto us.
May He of great majesty be gracious to us— He whose mouth is Agni Jātavedas, born from the performance of ritual acts, who, within the ocean, does not consume His own elements.
May He whose eye was the sun, the vehicle of the gods, consisting of the three Vedas, the abode of Brahman, be gracious to us.

May He of great majesty, who is the door to liberation, both immortality and death—may He be gracious unto us. From Whom the life-breath of all moving and non-moving beings arose, as well as vitality, strength, vigor, and Vāyu;
may He of great majesty, whom we follow like subjects following a sovereign emperor, be gracious unto us.

From whose ears the directions were born, from whose heart the cavities, and from whose navel the sky— may that Puruṣa of great majesty, whose banner is the subtle body composed of the vital breaths and senses, be gracious unto us.
From His strength came Mahendra, from His favor the gods, from His anger the Lord of the Mountains, and from His intellect Viriñca.
From his apertures came the Vedas, and from his penis the sages; may he of great majesty be gracious to us.
Śrī was from his chest, the ancestors from his shadow, Dharma from his breast, and Adharma from his back;
the heavens were from his head and the Apsarases from his pastimes; may he of great majesty be gracious to us.
From His mouth came the Brahmin and the sacred Veda; from His arms came the Kṣatriya and strength;
from His thighs came the Vaiśya and vigor; and from His feet came the Śūdra and the Vedas. May He of great opulence be gracious unto us.
From His lower lip came greed; from His upper lip, affection; from His nose, splendor; and from His touch, the desire for cattle.
Yama is from his eyebrows, while Kāla is born from his eyelashes; may he of great majesty be gracious to us.
They speak of substance, age, action, and the specific qualities ordained by his *yogamāyā*;
may he whose nature is difficult to conceive and who subverts the views of the awakened be gracious to us—may he of great majesty be gracious to us.

Salutations to Him whose power is perfectly tranquil, whose self is fulfilled by the attainment of sovereign bliss, who does not become attached to the modes of nature fashioned by *māyā* through His functions, and who is the messenger of the wind-god. As such, reveal Yourself to us, making Yourself the object of our senses.
O All-pervading Lord, for those who have surrendered and desire to behold Your lotus-face with a smile, You Yourself manifest at various times through diverse forms created by Your own will; indeed,
O Blessed One, You perform that very deed which is otherwise unbearable for us.
The actions of embodied beings afflicted by sense objects involve great suffering and yield little essence, or they are entirely fruitless; however, an action offered unto You is not so,
for even a lowly ritual act dedicated to the Lord does not result in failure.
For he alone is the beloved and beneficial Self of every person;
indeed, just as watering the root of a tree nourishes its trunk and branches,
so too does the worship of Viṣṇu benefit all beings and one's own self.
"Obeisances unto You, the infinite one, whose nature and actions are inconceivable; obeisances to the one beyond the modes, the lord of the modes, who now abides in the mode of goodness.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, when the Lord Hari, the Sovereign, was thus praised by the hosts of gods,
he appeared before them with the brilliance of a thousand rising suns;
by that very light, the eyes of all the gods were suddenly blinded.

The lordly Viriñca, together with Śarva, beheld that body— translucent, dark as emerald, with eyes as reddish as the interior of a lotus— and could not perceive the sky, the directions, the earth, nor himself, for how could he see the All-pervading Lord?
She was dressed in shimmering silken garments the color of molten gold;
her every limb was serene and beautiful, her face lovely and her eyebrows fair.
She was adorned with a crown of great jewels and two armlets.
She whose lotus-face possesses the beauty of cheeks illuminated by ear-ornaments,
who is adorned with a girdle, bracelets, necklaces,
and anklets, and who bears the Kaustubha jewel, the goddess Lakṣmī, wearing a garland of forest flowers.

Accompanied by all the hosts of immortals, with all their limbs touching the ground, Śiva— the foremost of the gods— along with his personified weapons such as the Sudarśana, praised the Supreme Puruṣa.
The venerable Brahmā said:

Obeisances, obeisances unto You, the Great-Souled One, who are unborn and yet the cause of birth, sustenance, and dissolution; who possess all qualities, yet are an ocean of the bliss of liberation; who are subtler than the subtlest, and whose abode is beyond calculation.

O Bull among Men, this form of Yours is to be worshipped by those seeking the highest good through both Vedic and Tantric yoga. O Creator, along with the three worlds, I behold everything within this Cosmic Form of Yours;
in You, who are self-dependent, was this universe in the beginning, in You it was in the middle, and in You it shall end.
You are the beginning, the end, and the middle of this world, just as clay is to a jar; You are beyond the beyond.
Having Yourself created this universe by means of Your own Māyā resting upon Yourself, You have entered into it.
The wise, possessed of insight, perceive You as devoid of qualities even amidst the interplay of the *guṇas*, through their minds disciplined in yoga.

Just as immortality is in fire, nectar in cows, food on earth, and water in the sky, so do men attain their livelihood through various means; indeed, the wise perceive You through the intellect within the modes of nature.
O Lord, we behold You now rising up—You whose lotus-navel has long been the object of our desire.

Having seen you, we have all today attained peace, like elephants afflicted by forest fires upon reaching the waters of the Gaṅgā. Therefore, O protector of all the worlds, please grant that for which we have come to the soles of your feet; for what else remains to be requested from you, the witness of all within and without?
"I and Śiva, as well as the gods beginning with Dakṣa, are like the flames of fire;
O Lord, what indeed do we know when we appear as separate entities? Grant us, the twice-born, the gods, and the mantras, that which is auspicious.
Śrī Śuka said:

Thus praised by Viriñca and the others, the Lord of the gods, having understood their hearts exactly as they were, spoke with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud to those who stood with palms joined in reverence, their senses fully withdrawn;
"In that task of the gods, there is but one sovereign."
Desiring to sport with them, [the Lord] spoke to them regarding the churning of the ocean and other such deeds.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Brahmā! O Śambhu! O gods! Listen to my words."
"Listen with focused attention, all you gods; it shall be for your ultimate welfare.
Go and establish a peace treaty with the Dānavas and Daityas, so long as they are favored by Time, until your own existence is secured."
"Even enemies must be allied with when there is a weighty purpose to be achieved; for even gods, O Lord, have followed the path of self-interest like the snake and the mouse.
Therefore, let an effort be made without delay to produce the nectar of immortality."
By drinking which, indeed, a living being seized by death becomes immortal;
having cast all creepers, grasses, vines, and herbs into the ocean of milk,
and having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope—

"O gods, with me as your ally, churn [the ocean] without weariness; the Daityas shall be the ones who endure the suffering, while you shall be the recipients of the fruit. O gods, approve of whatever the Asuras desire."
All purposes are not accomplished through agitation as they are through conciliation. You should not fear the Kālakūṭa poison born from the ocean;
you should never harbor greed or anger, but rather desire for the objects of the senses.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having thus instructed the gods, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama,
the Sovereign who moves according to His own will, disappeared from their sight.
Then, having offered obeisances to the Blessed One, the Grandfather (Brahmā) and Bhava (Śiva) departed for their respective abodes; and the gods approached Bali,
seeing that even though their enemies were not yet arrayed for battle, their own leaders were already agitated.
The king of the Daityas, who was worthy of praise and skilled in knowing the proper times for peace and war, forbade them;
yet they approached Virocana, who sat there protected by the leaders of the Asura hosts and endowed with supreme splendor, having conquered all.
The high-minded Mahendra, having consoled him with gentle words,
spoke all that which he had learned from Puruṣottama;
that was pleasing to the Daitya and to the other lords of the asuras who were present there.
Śambara, Ariṣṭanemi, and those who dwell in Tripura—
then the gods and asuras, having established an alliance and formed a bond of friendship,
made a supreme effort for the sake of the nectar, O scorcher of the foe.
Then, roaring and full of pride, those powerful ones with arms like iron clubs uprooted Mount Mandara by their sheer strength and carried it to the ocean;
however, Indra, Virocana, and the others grew weary from the exhaustion of carrying that distant burden.
Unable to bear its weight, they helplessly abandoned it on the path;
falling there, that golden mountain crushed many gods and demons with its immense mass.
Perceiving them to be thus dejected in mind, with their arms, thighs, and necks broken,
the Blessed One whose banner bears Garuḍa appeared there;
he beheld the gods and Dānavas crushed by the fall of the mountain.
By his mere glance, he restored the gods to life, free from decay and without wounds; then, having playfully placed Mount Mandara upon Garuḍa with a single hand,
he ascended and set out for the ocean, surrounded by hosts of gods and demons.
Having set down the mountain from his shoulder, Suparṇa, the best of those who fly,
was dismissed by Hari and went away, leaving it at the edge of the water.
Śrī Śuka said:

O best of the Kurus, having addressed Vāsuki, the king of serpents, with a share of the fruit, and having bound him as a rope around that mountain, the gods, filled with joy and exerting themselves for the sake of the nectar, began their work by making the ocean their boundary.
Hari seized the head first, and then the gods followed;
the lords of the Daityas did not desire that deed of the Great Person. "We will not seize the tail, which is an inauspicious limb of Hari," they said.
"Endowed with Vedic study and learning, and renowned for their births and deeds"—
seeing the Daityas standing thus in silence, the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu), together with the gods,
smiled and, letting go of the tip, seized the tail.

Having thus divided their positions, those sons of Kaśyapa, exerting themselves for the sake of the nectar, churned the ocean of milk. As the ocean was being churned, that mountain, being without support, sank into the waters.
O son of Pāṇḍu, although they were supported by the powerful [Yadus] out of respect,
their minds became utterly despondent and the beauty of their faces faded,
for their own prowess had been destroyed by an exceedingly mighty destiny.
Having observed the ritual of the Lord of Obstacles, the Lord of unassailable power and unfailing resolve assumed a great and wondrous tortoise form; entering the waters, he lifted up the mountain.
Seeing that king of mountains raised once more, the gods and demons prepared to churn it again.
With his back, which extended for a hundred thousand *yojanas* like another vast island,
he supported that mountain; O dear one, as it was shaken by the strength of the arms of the lords of the gods and demons and was revolving upon his back,
the immeasurable Primeval Tortoise perceived its turning as a mere scratching of his body.

Likewise, Viṣṇu entered the Asuras in an asura-form, stimulating their strength and heroism; and in a divine form, he inflamed the hosts of gods. Being in the form of the serpent-king Ananta, he who possesses a thousand arms, like another king of mountains, stepped upon Indra above with his hand.

He stood in the heavens, showered with flowers by the gods led by Brahmā, Bhava, and Indra, who were chanting his praises. Strengthened by the Supreme Lord, who entered both their eyes and their hearts from above and below,
those intoxicated with joy vigorously churned the ocean— whose circles of crocodiles were agitated— with the great mountain.

The asuras— Pauloma, Kāleya, Bala, Ilvala, and others— their splendor struck down by the smoke from the fire of the breaths issuing from the mouths of a thousand fierce glances of the Lord of Serpents,
became like sarala trees consumed by a forest fire.
And the gods, their radiance eclipsed by the flames of that breath, had their garments, garlands, crowns, armor, and faces turned smoky-grey.

The clouds, obedient to the Lord, rained down, and winds were driven by the waves of the ocean. When nectar did not emerge despite the ocean being churned by the leaders of the hosts of gods and asuras, the Unconquered One himself performed the churning.
Dark as a rain cloud, with a golden halo, with lightning flashing from his ears,
with disheveled hair shining upon his head, wearing a garland, and with red eyes;
holding a venomous serpent with his victorious arms that grant fearlessness to the world.
Churning with the churning-stick, he then shone like Mount Mandara holding up the mountain;
from the ocean being churned, first there arose a most terrible and fierce poison named Hālāhala,
amidst the waters teeming with agitated fish, crocodiles, serpents, tortoises, whales, elephants, sharks, and timingilas.
O dear one, as that unbearable and irresistible force of terrible velocity spread through every direction, above and below, and surged upward,

the terrified beings— including the lords— finding themselves unprotected, fled for refuge to Sadāśiva. They beheld him, the best of gods, who was desired by the Goddess for the welfare of the three worlds and by the sages.
They prostrated with hymns of praise before him as he sat upon a mountain, practicing austerities for the sake of liberation.
The illustrious Prajāpatis said:
"O God of gods, O Great God, O Soul of all beings, O Creator of all beings!"
"Save us, who have sought refuge in you, from the poison that consumes the three worlds!
You alone are the Lord of the entire universe regarding both bondage and liberation;
therefore, the wise worship you, the Guru who removes the suffering of those who have taken refuge."
O All-pervading One, when You, the Self-seeing, assume the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva through Your own power consisting of the *guṇas* to effect the creation, maintenance,
and dissolution of this universe, O Infinite One, You are the supreme, secret Brahman, the source of the conception of both being and non-being.
O Lord of the universe, You are the Self who shines forth through manifold powers.
You are the source of sound, the origin of the world, the Self, the life-force, the senses, the material elements, their qualities, and inherent nature.
You are time, sacrifice, truth, and immortality; You are dharma, and that which they declare as the imperishable, the threefold Veda, all resides within You.
Fire is Your mouth, for You are the self of all deities; they know the earth to be the lotus-feet of the world’s source;

Time is Your movement, for You are the self of all deities; the quarters are Your ears, and the Lord of Waters is Your tongue. The sky is Your navel, the wind is Your breath, the sun is Your eyes, and water is Your semen.
O Blessed One, the Supreme and the Lower Self take refuge in You; the Moon is Your self, the mind is the sky, and the head is Yours.

The oceans are Your belly, the mountains are the collection of Your bones, and all herbs and creepers are Your body hairs. The Vedic meters are Your seven constituent elements in person, O Embodiment of the Three Vedas, and all dharma is Your heart.
O Lord, the five Upaniṣads are Your faces, by which the collection of thirty-eight mantras is formed;
that supreme reality called Śiva is You Yourself, O God, who abide as self-luminous light.
Your shadow resides within the waves of unrighteousness, while Your three eyes are the emissions of the qualities of goodness, passion, and darkness.
The Sāṅkhya, the Self, the author of the scripture, Your vision; the Lord consisting of the Vedic meters, the ancient seer—

O Girīśa, protector of all worlds, that supreme light of Yours is not accessible even to Viriñca, Vaikuṇṭha, or the lord of the gods, wherein neither rajas, nor tamas, nor sattva exists, and which is Brahman, devoid of all differentiation.
That [praise] is not sufficient for Your glorification, who destroy many malevolent beings such as Kāma, Adhvara, Tripura, and Kālagara; rather,
it is that which You Yourself created with Your own eye at the time of universal dissolution.
He does not even perceive the ash smeared upon him by the crest of a spark from a fire;
yet he is one whose feet are meditated upon in the heart by those teachers who delight in the Self,
and who performs dualistic conduct with Umā while being intensely heated by austerity.
Wailing fiercely and harshly, devoted to the cremation ground,
those shameless ones have surely found refuge in you—
refuge that is beyond both the existent and the non-existent, and beyond the supreme.

Even Brahmā and the other gods are not capable of directly perceiving the true nature of the Infinite One; how much less so can we praise Him? We possess only a mere fraction of power, pertaining to the creation of His creation.
"O Maheśvara, we behold this supreme form of Yours, but not Your higher [nature];
for You, whose actions are unmanifest, have manifested Yourself for the sake of blessing the world.
Śrī Śuka said:
Seeing that calamity of theirs, the god who is a friend to all beings was deeply pained with compassion; he spoke thus to his virtuous and beloved wife. Śrī Śiva said:

"Alas! Behold this slaughter of living beings, O Bhavānī, brought about by the Kālakūṭa poison arising from the churning of the Ocean of Milk. Indeed, I must grant safety to these who desire to preserve their lives."
For this indeed is the purpose of the Lord: the protection of the distressed.
While living beings are deluded by His own illusory power (*māyā*) and harbor mutual enmity, the saintly protect other creatures even at the cost of their own lives, which are as fragile as a moment.
"O blessed lady, when a person acts with compassion, Hari, the Self of all, is pleased.
When the Blessed Lord Hari is pleased, I, along with all that is moving and unmoving, am pleased.
Therefore, I shall consume this poison; may there be well-being for my subjects."
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus addressed Bhavānī, the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, began to consume that poison; she, knowing his power, gave her consent.
Then, having taken the all-pervading *hālāhala* poison into the palm of his hand, Mahādeva, the creator of beings, consumed it out of compassion; thereupon,
the one whose impurities were washed away by water displayed his own prowess to him as well.
That which He made blue upon His throat is the ornament of the virtuous;
for generally, virtuous people suffer on account of the suffering of the world.
Indeed, that is the supreme worship of the Supreme Person, the Self of all.
Having heard of that deed of Śambhu, the God of gods, the bountiful one,
the progeny of Dakṣa’s daughter, Brahmā, and Vaikuṇṭha offered their praises;
for they had seized whatever little had spilled from his hand as he drank.
The scorpions, snakes, and other venomous creatures that were like poisonous herbs [were neutralized].
Śrī Śuka said:
When the poison was drunk by the one whose emblem is the bull (Śiva), those gods and demons were delighted.
They churned the ocean with great force, and from it the sacrificial vessel (havirdhānī) emerged;
O King, the sages who discourse on Brahman took possession of that vessel as the fire-offering cow (agnihotrī) for the sake of the pure oblation of the sacrifice that leads to the gods.
From that [egg] emerged the horse named Uccaiḥśravas, white as the moon; Bali desired it, but Indra did not, by the instruction of the Lord. Then Airāvata, the king of elephants, emerged.
With his four tusks, he took away the splendor of the white mountain;
from that, O King, the eight elephants of the quarters, beginning with Airāvaṇa, were born,
as well as the eight female elephants, beginning with Abhramu.
From the great ocean there arose a gem called Kaustubha, a ruby;
Hari desired that jewel for the ornamentation of his chest.
Thereafter, the Pārijāta tree appeared, the adornment of the world of the gods.
Just as you always satisfy those who seek wealth on this earth with their desires,
from that [act] were born celestial nymphs, adorned with golden necklaces and fine garments,
delightful to the inhabitants of heaven by their charming movements, playfulness, and glances.
Then Śrī Ramā, devoted to the Blessed Lord, appeared in person,
coloring the quarters with her splendor like a flash of lightning from the clouds;
all beings, including gods, asuras, and humans, felt a longing for her.
Mahendra brought a magnificent and wonderful throne for her, whose mind was captivated by his beauty, nobility, youth, complexion,
and majesty; and the most excellent rivers, personified, brought pure water in golden jars.

The earth, for the purpose of the consecration, brought forth all medicinal herbs; the cows provided the five purifying substances; and the two months of Madhu and Mādhava (Vaiśākha) served as the spring season. The sages then prepared the ceremonial bath according to the prescribed rites.
The Gandharvas sang auspicious songs and the dancers danced;
the clouds resounded with the tumultuous sounds of mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, murajas, ānakas, and gomukhas, as well as conchs, flutes, and lutes.

Then the elephants of the quarters, with vessels full of water and Vedic hymns recited by the twice-born, consecrated the virtuous goddess Śrī, who held a lotus in her hand. The ocean presented her with two garments of yellow silk.

Varuṇa gave him the Vaijayantī garland, with bees intoxicated by its honey; Viśvakarman, the lord of creatures, gave him various ornaments; Sarasvatī gave him a necklace; Aja gave him a lotus; and the Nāgas gave him earrings.
Then, having taken with her hand the lotus garland from which bees were humming— after the rites for auspiciousness had been performed—
the slender-waisted woman moved along, bearing a most beautiful face adorned with fine earrings on her lovely cheeks and a bashful smile;
her two breasts were even and close together, anointed with sandalwood and saffron.
Moving here and there with the lovely tinkling of her anklets, she shone like a golden vine;
looking for her own faultless station— eternal and endowed with unfailing virtues—
she found none among the Gandharvas, Siddhas, Asuras, Yakṣas, Cāraṇas, or the inhabitants of the celestial realm.
Surely his austerity was such that it did not conquer his anger; and his knowledge, wherever it existed, was not free from attachment.
He possessed some greatness, yet he had no conquest over his desires; how could such a one be a true lord, depending as he did on another?
His dharma, wherever it was found, lacked kindness toward all beings; and his renunciation, wherever it occurred, was not the cause of liberation.
A man possesses no valor that is not produced by the force of speed, for there is no second [quality] free from attachment to the *guṇas*.

Longevity does not exist anywhere without auspicious character (*śīla-maṅgala*), nor does even that [longevity] exist without being known through one's lifespan. Where both [vigor and longevity] are found, he is indeed auspicious; who, moreover, would not desire me, who am the most auspicious?

Having thus reflected, Ramā chose as her boon Mukunda— the refuge of all qualities who, by virtue of his unfailing excellent attributes, is the sole shelter for her, desired by all virtues yet himself free from desire—
placing upon his shoulder a beautiful garland of fresh lotuses.
He stood placing his own abode near her breast, which was resonant with the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees;
she departed with eyes blossoming with a bashful smile.
The chest of that Śrī— the mother of the progenitor of the three worlds— became the supreme abode of her own supreme manifestation;
for Śrī gazed upon her own offspring with a compassionate look.
Standing there, they strengthened the three worlds along with their presiding deities;
meanwhile, a vast sound arose from the conches, trumpets, drums, and other musical instruments,
as well as from the gods and their followers, who were dancing and singing together with their wives.
Brahmā, Rudra, Aṅgiras, and the other leaders— all the creators of the universe— praised the All-pervading Lord with unfailing mantras indicative of His nature, as they showered down flowers.
The gods, along with the Prajāpatis and all living beings, were beheld by Śrī.

Endowed with virtues such as good character and the like, they attained supreme bliss. But when the Daityas and Dānavas became devoid of strength, greedy, lacking in effort, shameless, and neglected by Lakṣmī, O King—
Then there appeared the goddess Vāruṇī, a lotus-eyed maiden;
by the permission of Hari, the Asuras indeed seized her.
Then, from the ocean being churned by the sons of Kaśyapa who were seeking the nectar of immortality—
O Great King, there arose a most wonderful person:
one with long, thick, staff-like arms, a shell-like neck, and reddish-brown eyes;
he was dark-complexioned, youthful, wearing a garland, and adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in yellow garments, broad-chested, with well-polished jeweled earrings,
his hair-ends glossy and curled, he was handsome and possessed the prowess of a lion;
adorned with bracelets, he bore a jar filled with nectar.
He was indeed born from a portion of a portion of the Lord Viṣṇu himself;
known as Dhanvantari, he was the seer of Āyurveda and a recipient of sacrificial offerings.
Beholding him and the pitcher filled with nectar, all the Asuras [seized it].
Desiring all things for themselves, they forcibly seized the jar;
while that jar, the vessel of nectar, was being carried away by the asuras,
the gods, dejected in mind, sought refuge in Hari.
Seeing their distress, the Blessed One, who fulfills the desires of His servants, said:
"Do not grieve; I shall accomplish your mutual purpose by My own power.
For the sake of that object, a dispute arose among them, as their minds were consumed by thirst for it.
"O Lord, 'I first! I first! Not you! Not you!'—thus the gods argue. Those who have exerted equal effort deserve their own share;
this is the eternal law in this sacrificial session, like a *sattra* sacrifice."
O King, having thus forbidden their own people, the sons of Diti, filled with envy and being weak themselves, repeatedly seized the jars from those who were stronger.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, the Lord who knows all means, [appeared].
She assumed an indescribable and most wonderful female form,
dark as a blue lotus to behold and beautiful in every limb;
she wore matching earrings, possessed lovely cheeks, and a prominent nose.
She possessed a waist made slender by the weight of her breasts, which had developed in the bloom of fresh youth;
her eyes were startled by the humming of bees attracted to the fragrance of her face;
and she bore a garland of full-blown jasmine flowers upon the mass of her beautiful hair.
Adorned with a necklace upon his neck and armlets upon his beautiful arms,
clothed in stainless garments that beautified the island of his hips with their girdle,
and possessing lovely, moving anklets upon his feet that shone brightly;
With glances accompanied by bashful smiles and the playful movement of his eyebrows,
he repeatedly kindled desire within the hearts of the leaders of the Daitya hosts.
Śrī Śuka said:

Those demons, having abandoned their friendship and seizing the vessel from one another, saw a woman approaching who was acting according to the ways of bandits; they cried out, "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what splendor! Oh, what fresh youth she possesses!"
Thus, their hearts filled with desire, they rushed toward her and asked:
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From where do you come, and what do you intend to do?
Whose are you, O lady of beautiful thighs? Tell us, for you seem to churn our very minds."
"We do not know of anyone— neither among the gods, daityas, siddhas, gandharvas,
cāraṇas, nor the lords of the worlds— who has ever touched you before, much less any human being.
O lady of beautiful brows, you have surely been sent by Fate to [tempt] embodied beings."
O compassionate one, why do you not bestow delight upon all our senses and minds? O proud lady of slender waist, grant welfare to us, your kinsmen who are locked in enmity over a single object.
"We are the brothers, the heirs of Kaśyapa, who have performed our manly duties; divide [the inheritance] according to the law so that no division may cause dissension.
Thus addressed by the Daityas, Hari assumed the form of a woman through his illusory power (*māyā*).
Smiling and gazing with beautiful sidelong glances, he spoke this;
the Blessed Lord said:
"How is it that you, the descendants of Kaśyapa, have united with me, a woman of loose conduct?"
A wise man never places his trust in lustful women; for the gods' enemies say that friendships with female jackals and with wanton women are transient, as they constantly seek newer and newer prey.
Śrī Śuka said: Thus,
their minds comforted by her playful jests, the asuras laughed with deep emotion and presented her with the vessel of nectar.
Then, taking the vessel of nectar, Hari spoke with a voice beautified by a slight smile:
"Whatever has been done by me for you—whether good or bad—if it is accepted, I shall divide this nectar among you.
Hearing these words spoken by him, the foremost of the asuras...
Those who understood the immeasurable nature of her [power] accepted it as being so.
Then, having fasted, bathed, and offered oblations of clarified butter into the fire,
and having given gifts to cows, Brahmins, and the destitute, they were consecrated with blessings by the twice-born.
Having each put on fresh garments according to their pleasure, they all, adorned with ornaments, sat down upon the *kuśa* grass whose tips pointed eastward,
while the gods and the sons of Diti were seated facing the east.

In that hall, which was perfumed with incense and graced with garlands and lamps, O King, she entered— she whose gait was languid due to the weight of her hips draped in fine white silk, whose eyes were unsteady with intoxication, who tinkled with the sound of golden anklets, whose breasts were like jars,
and who held a water-pot in her hand. She moved with a low murmur, her voice echoing like the jingling of golden ornaments.
Beholding her— the companion of Śrī, whose ears, nose, cheeks, and face were made beautiful by golden earrings, who was known as the Supreme Deity,
and whose breast-cloth had slipped away due to her smiling glance— the gods and demons were utterly bewildered.
The giving of nectar to the demons was like a wicked act toward serpents.
Considering them to be cruel by birth, Acyuta did not divide that [offering] among them;
rather, the Lord of the World, having arranged separate rows for both groups,
had them sit down in their respective rows.
Carrying the vessel, he deceived the Daityas with his movements and made those standing at a distance drink the nectar that removes old age and death.
O King, those Asuras remained faithful to the agreement they themselves had made.
Bound by affection, they remained silent out of a loathing for quarreling with women; having placed their deep trust in her, they were fearful of the loss of that intimacy,
and being constrained by great respect, they did not say anything unpleasant.
Disguised as a deity, Svarbhānu entered the assembly of the gods and drank the soma; being pointed out by the Moon and the Sun,
[Indra] struck off his head with a razor-edged discus while he was drinking.
Hari’s headless trunk, drenched with nectar, fell down; however,
the Unborn Lord (Aja) ordained immortality for the head and fashioned it into a planet that,
harboring enmity, pursues the moon and the sun during the lunar festivals.
When the nectar had been mostly drunk by the gods,
Lord Hari, the creator of the worlds, assumed his own form while the lords of the asuras were looking on.
Thus, the hosts of gods and asuras, [facing] equal place and time...
Even the differing views regarding cause, purpose, action, and intention result in various fruits;
therein, the hosts of gods directly attained immortality as their fruit,
whereas the Daityas did not, because they did not take refuge at the dust of His lotus feet.
Whatever is performed by men through their vital breaths, senses, actions, mind, and speech toward the body, children, and so forth, is unreal because of their separateness;
that which is performed by those very same things [toward the Self] is real because of their non-separateness.
"That which becomes the watering of the root of everything [is that].
Śrī Śuka said:
"O King, thus the Dānavas and Daityas did not find the nectar."
O King, those who were disciplined and diligent in their duties, yet turned away from Vāsudeva, prepared the nectar and, having caused their own gods to drink it,
he whose vehicle is Garuḍa departed while all living beings looked on.
Seeing the supreme prosperity of their rivals, those sons of Diti,
unable to endure it, rose up with weapons raised against the gods.
Then all the hosts of gods were invigorated by the drinking of the nectar of immortality.
Taking refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa, they fought back with their weapons;
there, O King, occurred a most terrible battle between the gods and the asuras,
tumultuous and hair-raising, on the shore of the ocean.
There, those rivals, their minds agitated in battle, encountered one another and struck each other with swords, arrows, and various weapons.
There was a great clamor of conchs, trumpets, mṛdaṅga drums, kettledrums, and ḍamaru drums.
The clamor of shouting elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry arose;
there, chariot-warriors engaged with chariot-warriors, infantrymen with infantrymen,
horses with horses, and elephants with elephants in the battle.
Some warriors fought with camels, some with elephants, and others with donkeys; some fought with white-faced bears, leopards, lions, and monkeys;
while others fought with vultures, herons, cranes, hawks, eagles, and timiṅgilas.
Some were with *śarabhas*, buffaloes, rhinoceroses, bulls, gayals, and red deer;
some with jackals, rats, chameleons, rabbits, and men; others with goats, black antelopes, swans, and boars.

O King, others with bodies transformed into various forms entered ahead and ahead of both armies— beings moving through water, on land, and in the air. O King, they were accompanied by variegated banners and spotless white parasols.
With great and costly diamond-staffs,
with fans made of yak-tail hair, with upper turbans tossed by the wind, with radiant armor and ornaments, and with shimmering, bright weapons that surpassed even the rays of the sun.
O son of Pāṇḍu, the two armies of the heroic gods and demons shone with their garlands of warriors like two oceans filled with aquatic creatures.
In that battle, Bali, the son of Virocana, was the commander-in-chief of the asuras.
O Lord, there was a celestial vehicle named Vaihāyasa, which moved at will and was fashioned by Maya; it was equipped with all the implements of war, composed of every marvel,
inconceivable and indescribable, appearing yet invisible.
Seated upon that foremost of celestial chariots and surrounded by the commanders of all his armies,
he shone like the moon at its rising, with yak-tail fans and a magnificent parasol.
On all sides of him were the Asura leaders of the hosts, traveling in their own vehicles.
Namuci, Śambara, Bāṇa, Vipracitti, Ayomukha,
Dvimūrdhan, Kālanābha, Praheti, Heti, Ilvala, Śakuni, Bhūtasantāpa, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and Virocana.
Hayagrīva, Śaṅkuśiras, Kapila, Meghadundubhi,
Tāraka, Cakradṛk, Śumbha, Niśumbha, Jambha, Utkala,
Ariṣṭa, Ariṣṭanemi, Maya, and Tripurādhipa.
Others— the Paulomas, Kāleyas, Nivātakavacas, and so forth—
received no portion of the Soma and were mere partakers of suffering;
all of them had been defeated many times by the immortals on the front lines of battle.
Uttering lion-roars, they blew their conchs with great sound; seeing his enemies thus arrogant, Indra, the slayer of Bala, became exceedingly enraged.
Mounted upon Airāvata, the elephant of the quarters, the sovereign of heaven shone resplendent.
Just as the sun, the lord of the day, rises over the mountain of sunrise with flowing springs,
so too were all the gods seated on every side around him, bearing various vehicles, banners, and weapons—
the world-protectors along with their hosts, including Vāyu, Agni, Varuṇa, and the others.
Charging at one another and striking each other in their vital parts, challenging and advancing forward, those warriors fought in pairs;
Bali fought with Indra, and Guha with Tāraka.
Varuṇa fought with Heti, O King, and Mitra with Praheti; Yama fought with Kālanābha, Viśvakarman with Maya,
Śambara with Tvaṣṭṛ, and Virocana with Savitṛ.
Aparājita fought with Namuci, the Aśvins with Vṛṣaparvan,
the god Sūrya with the hundred sons of Bali headed by Bāṇa,
Rāhu with Candra (the Moon), and Anila with Puloman.
The powerful goddess Bhadrakālī [slain] Niśumbha and Śumbha;
Vṛṣākapi [was slain] by Jambha; Vibhāvasu [by] Mahiṣa; and Ilvala, along with Vātāpi, [were slain] by the sons of Brahmā, O subduer of enemies.
Kāmadeva was overcome by Durmarṣa along with his mothers;
Bṛhaspati by Uśanas; and Śanaiścara by Naraka.
The Maruts were defeated by the Nivātakavacas, and the Vasu immortals by the Kāleyas.
The Viśvedevas fought with the Paulomas, and the Rudras with the Krodhavaśas. Thus, in that assembly, the Asuras and the lords of the gods, having joined together in pairs and engaging in combat,
encountered one another and struck with vigor, desiring victory with sharp arrows, swords, and *tomaras*.
With *bhuśuṇḍi* missiles, discuses, clubs, spears, *paṭṭiśa*s, javelins, torches, darts, axes,
swords, arrows, iron bars, mallets, and slings, they severed the heads [of the enemies].
Elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, along with their riders and mounts, were shattered in various ways.
With their arms, thighs, necks, and feet severed, and their banners, bows, armor, and ornaments cut away, they lay there;
then, from the battlefield crushed by the trampling of their feet and chariot wheels,
a thick cloud of dust arose, shrouding the quarters, the sky, and the sun, as it was drenched by streams of flowing blood.
The earth was strewn with those whose heads were adorned with tossing crowns and earrings, whose eyes were filled with fury, and whose lips were bitten;

with their great arms still bearing ornaments and weapons, and with thighs like the trunks of young elephants, that ground shone brilliantly. And there, headless trunks rose up, their eyes fixed upon the fallen heads.
Charging at the warriors in battle with his staff-like arms raised and brandishing weapons,
Bali struck Mahendra with ten arrows, Airāvata with three,
the four horses with four, and the charioteer with one.
As they were rushing toward him, Śakra, swift in his prowess,
cut them down with as many sharp arrows before they had even reached him, as if laughing;
beholding that supreme feat of his, he became indignant and took up his spear.
Hari cut down that blazing weapon, which resembled a great meteor and was held in her hand;
then a trident, then a spear, then a tomara-club, and whatever other weapon she might take up— the omnipresent Lord cut all of them down.
Then, having vanished from sight, the asura unleashed a demonic illusion (*asurī māyā*). Thereupon, O Lord, a mountain appeared above the host of the gods.
Then trees fell down, being consumed by a forest fire.
Rocks with jagged peaks pulverized the enemy force; great serpents, along with venomous vipers and scorpions, sprang forth;
and lions, tigers, boars, and massive elephants began to crush them.

And hundreds of Yātudhānīs, naked and with tridents in their hands, as well as hosts of Rākṣasas, O Lord, cried out, "Cut him! Pierce him! Then, great clouds appeared in the sky with deep and harsh sounds.
Struck by the winds, the thunderclouds released embers;
a vast fire, with the wind as its charioteer, was unleashed by the Daitya,
and like the fire of universal destruction (*sāṃvartaka*), it fiercely consumed the army of the gods.
Then the ocean was seen overflowing on all sides,
terrifying with waves and whirlpools tossed up by fierce winds.
Thus, in the battle, the Daityas possessed of great illusion remained invisible in their movements.
As the illusory powers were being unleashed, the soldiers of the gods became despondent; O King, Indra and the others did not know how to counter them.
Then, being meditated upon, the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, appeared there.

Then He was seen with His sprout-like feet resting upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, clad in saffron garments, with eyes like fresh collyrium, and eight arms bearing weapons; He shone with the glorious Kaustubha gem, an invaluable crown, and earrings.
Upon His entry, the illusions born of the wicked deeds of the demons perished through the majesty of that Great One.
Just as a dream vanishes upon waking, so too the remembrance of Hari brings liberation from all calamities.
Having seen [the enemy] in battle, Kālanemi, whose vehicle was a great elephant, brandished his trident and hurled it at the one whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
O King, the Lord of the three worlds, seizing that trident with ease as it fell upon Garuḍa’s head, struck the enemy along with his mount using it.

Mālī and Sumāli, who were exceedingly powerful in battle, fell when their heads were severed by the discus; then Mālyavat, having struck him with a fierce club, slew the lord of the Daṇḍakas, while the enemy of the demons cut off the head of the roaring foe. Śrī Śuka said:

Then the gods, Indra, Vāyu, and the others, having regained their senses through the supreme compassion of the Supreme Person, struck with great force those various enemies in battle by whom they had previously been overwhelmed. The Lord Pākaśāsana was enraged against the son of Virocana.
When he raised his thunderbolt, the people cried out, "Alas!
Alas! Vajrapāṇi said to him as he stood before him, having set aside that thunderbolt:
"O wise one, so well-endowed, wandering in the great battle..."
"O fool, like an actor, you seek to conquer us, the masters of illusion, by means of illusions.
Having defeated children whose eyes are bound, an actor carries off their wealth. Those who desire to ascend to heaven by means of illusions [only] wish to climb up."
"I shall shake off those ignorant bandits from their former station;
O dull-witted one, today with my hundred-edged thunderbolt I shall take away your head— prepare yourself along with your kinsmen!"
Śrī Bali said:
For those engaged in battle, their actions impelled by time,
fame, victory, defeat, and death shall all occur for everyone in due course.
The wise perceive this world as bound by the rope of time;
they neither rejoice nor grieve therein, whereas you are unwise.
We do not consider ourselves to be the means for those who merely imagine themselves to be so.
"We shall seize your words, which, though uttered by those worthy of praise, strike at our very vitals.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus rebuked the Lord, the hero, the crusher of warriors, [struck him] with iron arrows.
With full-drawn arrows and forceful strikes, he struck him again;
thus repulsed by his enemy who spoke the truth, the god could not endure that insult, like an elephant struck by a goad.
The supreme crusher hurled his infallible thunderbolt at him;
struck by it, he fell to the ground like a mountain with its wings severed.
Seeing his friend Jambha, the companion and ally of Bali, fallen, [the demon host was overcome].
Displaying friendship toward his friend even though he had been slain,
that one of great strength, mounted upon a lion, approached with speed, raised his mace,
and struck Śakra and the elephant on the collarbone.

Severely pained by the blow of the club and utterly overwhelmed, the elephant touched the earth with its knees and fell into a state of extreme exhaustion. Then Mātali brought forth a chariot yoked to one thousand bay horses.
Having been brought there, the Lord abandoned the elephant and mounted the chariot. Praising that deed of the charioteer, the best of the Dānavas,
smiling, struck him in the battle with his flaming spear.
Relying on his inner strength, Mātali endured pain that was most difficult to bear;
then Indra, filled with rage, struck off the head of Jambha with his thunderbolt.
Having heard from the sage Nārada that Jambha had been slain, his kinsmen [acted].
Namuci, Bala, and Pāka also arrived there with great haste;
afflicting Indra in his vital organs with harsh words,
they showered him with arrows as clouds drench a mountain with torrents of rain.
In that battle, Bala, being light-handed, simultaneously struck the thousand horses of Indra with as many arrows; likewise,
Pāka struck Mātali with two hundred and the chariot along with its various parts separately.
