That single act of aiming and releasing [the arrow] was a marvel in battle. Namuci, having struck him with fifteen great arrows feathered with gold, roared in the fray like a rain-cloud filled with water.
From all sides, the demons covered Indra, along with his chariot and charioteer, with heaps of arrows, just as clouds cover the sun during the rainy season;
unable to perceive him and being utterly overwhelmed, the hosts of gods along with their followers cried out in distress.
Like merchants on the ocean whose ship has been wrecked, they were leaderless and utterly defeated by the enemy force.
Then Turāṣāṭ, having emerged from the cage formed by his arrows, leading his horses, chariot, and banner,
shone like the sun at the end of the night, illuminating the quarters, the sky, and the earth with his own splendor.
Seeing his army being oppressed by the enemies in battle, the Lord,
the wielder of the thunderbolt, raised his vajra in rage to slay the foe.
With that very weapon, which had eight edges, he struck the heads of Bala and Pāka.
While his kinsmen looked on, O King, he carried him away, engendering fear; seeing that slaughter, Namuci was filled with grief, indignation,
and rage, and desiring to kill Indra, O ruler of men, he made a supreme effort.
Seizing an iron trident adorned with golden ornaments and bells,
he rushed forward in a rage, threatening him, "You are slain!
and bellowing like a lion, he hurled it at the king of the gods.
Then, as it fell through the sky with great speed, Hari cut it into a thousand pieces with his arrows.
O King, the Lord of the Gods, filled with rage, struck him on the neck with his thunderbolt, intending to sever his head.
Yet even that powerful thunderbolt, hurled by the strength of the Lord of the Suras, could not pierce even his skin.
That was a supreme wonder: that Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra of exceeding prowess, was humiliated by the skin from the neck of Namuci.
Because his thunderbolt had been repelled by his enemy, Indra was terrified, wondering, "What is this? By the power of fate, a phenomenon has occurred that bewilders the world."
By whom, at the end of the creation, the wings of the mountains were formerly lopped off as they settled upon the earth with the weight of their flying feathers;
by whom Vṛtra was split apart, he who possessed the essence of ascetic power and was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
There were others as well, endowed with strength and their skins unscarred by all weapons.
This very thunderbolt, though released by me against that insignificant asura, was repelled; I did not take up the staff, for even the spiritual power of a brāhmaṇa should not be used without cause.
To Śakra, who was thus despondent, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"This Dānava does not deserve death by either dry or wet means;
for I have granted him this boon that his death shall not come from anything wet or dry."
"Therefore, O Maghavan, you must consider another means against the enemy.
Having heard those divine words, Maghavan, being well-composed,
meditated and then beheld foam as a means that possessed the nature of both [the divine and the material].
He did not sever the head of Namuci with anything dry nor with anything wet.
The hosts of sages praised the Lord and showered Him with garlands.
Viśvāvasu and Parāvasu, the two chief Gandharvas, sang.
The celestial kettledrums resounded and the dancers danced with joy;
likewise, other adversaries such as Vāyu, Agni, Varuṇa, and the rest,
slaughtered the Asuras just as lions slay deer.
O King, sent by Brahmā, the divine sage Nārada saw the destruction of the Dānavas and restrained the gods. Śrī Nārada said:
"O you who have taken refuge in the arms of Nārāyaṇa, you have attained immortality; strengthened by Śrī, all of you desist from this conflict.
Śrī Śuka said:
Restraining their fury and indignation, and honoring the words of the sage,
they all departed for heaven while being praised by their followers;
those who remained behind in that battle did so with the approval of Nārada.
Taking Bali, who was lifeless, they went to the western mountain;
there, Uśanas restored him to life by means of his own science, the *saṃjīvanī*, so that his limbs were unimpaired and his neck remained intact.
And Bali, touched by Uśanas, regained his senses and memory;
though defeated, he did not grieve, for he was an expert in the true nature of the world.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having heard this, Hari, whose banner bears the bull, having deluded the hosts of gods by means of the form of a woman, caused them to drink the Soma;
then Giriśa, mounted upon his bull and surrounded by all the hosts of living beings, departed.
Accompanied by his goddess, he went to see where Madhusūdana was staying; there,
Śiva, having been honored with great respect by the Blessed One and Umā,
sat down comfortably and, after returning the honors, spoke thus to Hari with a smile.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O God of gods, pervader of the universe, Lord of the world, composed of the world; You are the Self of all beings, their cause, and their sovereign.
That which is its beginning, end, and middle; that which is other than this, and that which is outside—since these do not belong to You, the immutable, You are that Truth, Brahman, the Consciousness.
Desiring the highest good and free from worldly desires, [they seek] Your very lotus feet.
Having abandoned attachment to both [the material and the spiritual], the sages worship You,
who are the perfect Brahman— immortal, devoid of the three modes of nature, free from sorrow,
consisting of pure bliss, changeless, and both non-different and different [from all else].
You alone are the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe;
you are the Self and the Lord, independent because all else depends upon you.
You alone are the one reality, both the dualistic world of being and non-being and the non-dual Absolute.
Just as gold remains the same whether fashioned into an ornament or left unworked, there is no difference in its substance;
yet, due to ignorance, people have conceived a distinction regarding You,
for You are beyond all limiting conditions and the transformation of qualities.
Some perceive You as Brahman, others as Dharma;
some as the Supreme Person, the Lord beyond both being and non-being; and others perceive You as the Supreme endowed with ninefold power.
Some [know] the Great Person, the imperishable, who is self-dependent;
neither I, nor the Ṛṣis whose life-span is supreme, nor Marīci and the other chief progenitors of beings know Him who has indeed fashioned all things.
O Lord, those such as Daityas and mortals whose minds are stolen by Your māyā— how much more so those whose conduct is eternally unwholesome— are unable to perceive this, namely,
Your desired activity of maintenance, birth, and destruction. You alone are that.

Just as the wind enters both the sky and all that is called moving and non-moving, you comprehend the welfare of beings and the liberation from the bondage of worldly existence for the entire world by virtue of being its very self.
I have seen Your incarnations as You sported with Your divine qualities;
now I desire to see that which was assumed by You as a female form,
by which the Daityas were utterly deluded and the gods were made to drink the nectar of immortality.
"We have come desiring to see him, for our curiosity is great.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus entreated by the wielder of the trident, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu...
Laughing with profound emotion, he addressed Giriśa;
the Blessed Lord said:
"Out of curiosity for the sake of the Daityas, I assumed the form of a woman."
"O best of gods, since the vessel of nectar has departed while you were looking on at the tasks of the demigods,
I shall show it to you, for you desire to see it. To those possessed by lust, the arising of the fruit born of their own mental constructs is considered very significant."
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there;
and Bhava remained with Umā, casting his gaze in every direction.

Then, in a grove where the trees were covered with wonderful flowers and reddish shoots, he beheld an exquisite woman sporting with a ball; her hips were encircled by a girdle over shimmering silk garments,
and at every step, her breasts trembled from her turning and twisting movements, while her heavy, excellent necklaces swayed.
Her sprout-like feet seemed to break apart as they moved from side to side;
her long, tremulous eyes were intensely agitated by the restlessness of a ball spinning in every direction;
and her face was adorned with dark locks of hair upon cheeks that shone with earrings glittering on her ears.
Seeing her— whose silk garment was slipping and whose braid was disheveled— as she adjusted it with her beautiful left hand while striking a ball with her other hand,
thus bewildering the world with her divine power of illusion (māyā),
the Lord was captivated by her sidelong glance released with a slight smile of bashfulness during her play with the ball.
With his mind overwhelmed by gazing at and being gazed upon by the women, he did not perceive himself, Umā, or his own attendants nearby.
When the ball fell a great distance from the tip of her hand, the wind carried away the light garment and its cord from the woman who was following it, even as the god Bhava looked on.
Having thus beheld her— whose outer corners were beautiful, who was lovely to look upon, and enchanting to the mind— Bhava indeed set his heart upon her as she became attached to him;
his discernment was carried away by her, and he was overwhelmed by the god of love she had aroused.
Even as Bhavānī looked on, he went to her place, devoid of shame.
Seeing him approaching, she, naked and deeply ashamed, hid herself among the trees; laughing, she did not remain where she was.

The Blessed Lord Bhava, his senses stolen away and brought under the sway of desire, pursued her like a leader of an elephant herd pursuing a female elephant. Having followed her with great speed, he seized the woman against her will.
Having approached him, she bound his hair and embraced him with both arms;
thus embraced by the Blessed One, like a female elephant by a male elephant,
she moved here and there with her hair disheveled.
Having freed herself from the arms of that bull among the gods, O dear one,
that illusory woman of broad hips fled;
Rudra then pursued the path of Viṣṇu, whose deeds are miraculous.
Overcome by desire as if by an enemy, he fell [into a swoon]; as he was pursuing her, the seed of that man of unfailing virility spilled,
like that of a powerful bull-leader chasing after a cow in heat.
O lord of the earth, wherever the seed of that Great-Souled One fell upon the ground, those places became fields of silver and gold—
among rivers, lakes, mountains, forests, and groves.

Wherever the ṛṣis were present, there Hara was also present. O best of kings, when his semen had been discharged, he perceived himself to have been rendered inert by the divine illusion (māyā) of the Lord; thus he withdrew from that state of dejection.

Then, having understood the majesty of the Self, who is the soul of the universe and whose prowess is inscrutable, he no longer considered that [display] to be a wonder. Observing him to be unperturbed and free from shame, Madhusūdana—
Extremely pleased, the Blessed Lord, assuming his own personal form, spoke:
The Blessed Lord said:
"By good fortune, O best of the wise, you have remained steadfast in your own devotion through your own effort."
O dear one, since even I was freely deluded by your illusory power in the form of a woman,
what man other than you— who is himself attached— could ever cross over my *māyā*,
which emits various states of being and is insurmountable for those who have not disciplined their minds?
"This Māyā, composed of the modes of nature, shall not overcome you when she is joined by me, who am Time itself, acting in my various portions. Śrī Śuka said:

O King, having been thus honored by the Blessed One who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, Lord Bhava took leave of him, circumambulated him, and departed for his own abode along with his retinue; so too did the Blessed One depart from Bhavānī, who was his own portion manifested as Māyā.
O descendant of Bharata, he then spoke with affection to the eminent sages who were present:

"O friends, have you perceived the illusory power (*māyā*) of the unborn Supreme Person, the supreme deity? Even I, though the foremost among the parts [of that power], am deluded by it and lack self-control; what then of others who are not independent?"
"You, having approached me through yoga when I had indeed ceased [from activity] at the end of a thousand ages, have asked about Me;
this is that very Ancient Person (Puruṣa), wherein Time does not enter and where the Veda does not reach.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, O dear one, the prowess of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow has been described to you—
by whom the great mountain was borne upon his back during the churning of the ocean.
For one who repeatedly recites or hears this, no undertaking will ever fail.

The description of the qualities of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), which removes all the weariness of worldly existence, reached the ears of the gods— the foremost of the immortals— who had taken refuge at His feet that transcend the realm of the unreal and are accessible only through devotion; it nourished them like the nectar churned from the ocean.
I bow to Him who, assuming the deceptive guise of a young woman, deluded the enemies of the gods,
and who fulfills the desires of those who have approached Him.
Śrī Śuka said:
Manu, the son of Vivasvat, is known as Śrāddhadeva;
he is the seventh Manu currently existing—now hear from me about his offspring:
Ikṣvāku, Nabhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti.
Nariṣyanta, then Nābhāga, and the seventh is called Diṣṭa;
Tarūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and the tenth is remembered as Vasumān—
these, O scorcher of foes, are the ten sons of Vaivasvata Manu.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts;
the two Aśvins, the Ṛbhus, O King, and among them Indra, the destroyer of cities;
Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Gautama.

Jamadagni and Bharadvāja are remembered as the seven ṛṣis. Here too, the birth of the Blessed One occurred from Kaśyapa and Aditi; he was the youngest of the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Vāmana.
I have briefly described to you these seven *manvantaras*;
now I shall speak of those yet to come, which are likewise endowed with the power of Viṣṇu. And Vivasvat had two wives, both daughters of Viśvakarman.
O King of kings, regarding those two previously mentioned to you, Saṃjñā and Chāyā—the third, some say, is Vaḍavā. Of these, Saṃjñā had three sons:
Yama, Yamī, and Śrāddhadeva. Now hear of the sons of Chāyā.
Sāvarṇi’s daughter Tapatī was the wife of Saṃvaraṇa;
Śanaiścara was the third [son], and the two Aśvins were the sons of Vaḍavā.
When the eighth Manvantara arrives, Sāvarṇi will be the Manu.
O King, Nirmoka, Virajaska, and others will be the sons of Sāvarṇi.
There, the gods will be Sutapas, Virajas, and Amṛtaprabha.
Among them, Bali, the son of Virocana, will become Indra.
Having given these three paces to Viṣṇu when he was begging for them,
and having abandoned the perfected station of Indra, he will thereafter attain perfection—
he who was again bound in Sutala by the Lord, who was pleased with him.
Now, having been established in a realm superior even to heaven, he dwells like a sovereign god;
so too do the radiant Gālava, Rāma, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa,
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, our father, and the venerable Bādarāyaṇa.

By their own yogic power, these will become the Seven Sages there; at present, O King, they reside each in his own circle of hermitages. From Devaguhyā on the Sarasvatī, the lord Sārvabhauma [will arise].
The Lord, having taken away the position from Purandara, will give it to Bali.
The ninth Manu will be Dakṣasāvarṇi, born of Varuṇa;
O King, Bhūtaketu, Dīptaketu, and others will be his sons.
The gods will be headed by Pārā, Marīcigarbha, and others; Indra is known as Adbhuta.
There, the sages will be led by Dyutimat and others. From Āyuṣmat, in the city of Ambudhārā, shall arise Ṛṣabha, who is a portion (kalā) of the Blessed Lord.
By whom the wonderful Manu Daśama, the son of Upaśloka, will become the Brahmasāvarṇi Manu, by whom he shall enjoy the three worlds once they have been fully perfected;
his sons will be Bhūriṣeṇa and others, and the twice-born will be headed by Haviṣmat.
O twice-born ones, at that time Haviṣmān, Sukṛta, Satya, Jaya, Mūrti, Suvāsana, Viruddha, and others will be the gods; Śambhu will be the lord of the gods,
and Viṣvaksena will form a friendship with Śambhu in the region of Viṣūcī.
The all-pervading Lord, the creator of the universe, was born by his own portion in the house of Viśvasṛj as the self-controlled Manu Dharmasāvarṇi, the eleventh;
and his ten sons, Satyadharma and the others, are yet to come.
The birds there could travel at will, and the gods were devoted to the quest for liberation;
Indra was their presiding deity, as were the sages beginning with Aruṇa.
There, the son of Āryaka was known as Dharmasētu.
During the *vaidhṛti* conjunction, a portion of Hari will sustain the three worlds;
O King, Rudrasāvarṇi will be the twelfth Manu,
and Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and others will be his sons.
There, Ṛtadhāman will be Indra, along with the gods beginning with Harita;
the sages will be Tapomūrti and the ascetics beginning with Āgnīdhraka;
and the portion of Hari known as Svadhāma will bring about the success of that Manu’s mind.
The son of Satyasahasra and Sunṛtā will be the powerful Manu,
the thirteenth, known as Devasāvarṇi, who is self-possessed.
Citrasena, Vicitra, and others will be born from the body of Devasāvarṇi.
The gods will then be known as Sukarman and Sutāman, and Indra will be Divaspati.
The sages at that time will be Nirmoka, Tattvadarśa, and others.
Upahartṛ will be the son of Devahotra and the lord of heaven.
The Lord of Yoga, an expansion (aṃśa) of Hari, will be born of Bṛhatī;
he will become the fourteenth Manu, Indrasāvarṇi.
Those such as Urugambhīrabuddhi and others will be born from the prowess of Indrasāvarṇi.
The gods will be the Pavitras and the Cākṣuṣas; Indra will be Śuci;
Agni will be Bāhu; and Śuci and Śuddha, along with the Māgadhas and others, will be ascetics.
At that time, Hari will be Bṛhadbhānu, the son of Satrāyaṇa.
O great king, in this sacrificial canopy, the threads of ritual action have been spread out.
O King, these fourteen [manvantaras] have been described to you as following through the three periods of time; measured by these, a kalpa consists of a cycle of one thousand yugas.
The King said:
O Blessed One, please tell me how these Manu and others were appointed to their respective duties within the various Manvantaras, and by whom they were assigned to which specific tasks.
The venerable sage said:
O lord of the earth, the Manus, the sons of Manu, the sages,
the Indras, and the hosts of gods— all are subject to the command of the Supreme Person.
O King, those forms of the Supreme Person described as sacrifice and so forth—
by these, Manu and others are impelled to maintain the course of the world.
Just as at the end of the four ages, the collections of the Vedas are swallowed by Time, [so too are the worlds withdrawn].

By means of austerity, the sages perceived that from which eternal dharma originates; from that, O King, the Manus, instructed by Hari, properly cause the four-footed dharma to circulate upon the earth at their respective times.
The protectors of the subjects guarded them according to their respective divisions until the end;
the gods, who partake in the sacrificial portions, and those who were associated with them there, [enjoyed the fruit].
Indra [obtained] the exalted glory of the three worlds bestowed by the Blessed One.

While enjoying [the fruits of his past deeds], Hari protects the three worlds; at will, he rains down upon the world. Assuming the form of a perfected being (*siddha*), he imparts knowledge according to the age (*yuga*). Bearing the form of a seer (*ṛṣi*), he reveals ritual action (*karman*); bearing the form of the Lord of Yoga (*yogeśvara*), he reveals yoga.

In the form of the Lord of Creatures, He brings forth creation; in the form of the Sovereign, He slays the wicked; and in the form of Time, He brings about the destruction of all through His distinct qualities.
Thus, by means of His illusory power consisting of name and form, He is praised by these people.

It is not perceived by those whose minds are deluded by various philosophical systems. This is proclaimed to be the measure of a kalpa and its subdivisions, wherein those who know the past speak of fourteen manvantaras.
The King said: Why did Hari ask Bali for three paces of land?
And why did the Lord of Beings, though he had already obtained his desired object, bind him like a wretch?
"We wish to know this, for our curiosity is great:
how the Lord of Sacrifice, who is perfect and sinless, came to be bound.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been deprived of his fortune and his life-breaths by Indra, Bali was restored to life by the Bhṛgus.
With his whole being, Bali devoted himself to those Bhṛgus as their disciple by offering them his very self.
Then the Bhṛgu brahmins, being well-pleased, caused him to perform the Viśvajit sacrifice, whereby he ascended to the third heaven.
Having consecrated him according to the prescribed rites with the great royal inauguration (*mahābhiṣeka*),
those of great majesty [prepared for him] a chariot bound with golden bands, horses as beautiful as tawny steeds,
and a banner resplendent with a lion, which had been obtained from the Fire-god through oblations.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) gave him a divine bow bound with gold, two quivers, and divine armor; and Śukra gave him a garland of unfading flowers and a lotus.
Thus, having been provided with the means for battle acquired by the brahmins and having had rites for his welfare performed by them, he then [honored] the brahmins.

Having circumambulated him and offered his salutations, he addressed Prahlāda and paid his respects. Then that great chariot-warrior, wearing beautiful garlands, having equipped himself with armor, and bearing a bow, a sword, and quivers, ascended the divine chariot given by Bhṛgu.
With arms adorned with golden armlets and shimmering shark-shaped earrings,
he shone as he mounted his chariot like the sacrificial fire upon its altar,
accompanied by the leaders of the Daitya hosts who were equal to him in sovereignty, strength, and splendor.
With his eyes as if drinking up the sky and burning as if consuming the horizons,
the Lord drew along the vast demonic army and proceeded toward the prosperous city of Indra, making heaven and earth tremble as it were.
It was beautiful with splendid groves and gardens such as Nandana,
filled with pairs of warbling birds and singing, intoxicated bees,
and celestial trees whose branches were heavily laden with sprouts, fruits, and flowers.
There, lotus ponds filled with flocks of swans, cranes, ruddy geese,
and ducks serve as playgrounds for the women attended by the gods; these ponds are encircled by the divine celestial Gaṅgā, which forms their moat.
It was adorned with a high wall the color of fire and provided with watchtowers, featuring doors with golden panels and crystal gateways,
with well-divided main roads, constructed by Viśvakarman.
It was rich with assembly halls, courtyards, and streets, and filled with tens of millions of celestial palaces; it possessed crossroads made of jewels with altars of diamond and coral,
where women of perpetual youth and beauty dwelt, dressed in stainless garments.
The noble ladies shine with beauty like fires with their flames;
there, the breeze blows along the path carrying the fragrance of fresh *saugandhika* garlands fallen from the hair of celestial women.
The beloved of the gods travel along paths covered by white smoke, fragrant with aloe-wood, issuing from the eyes of golden lattices;
the path is further enveloped by pearl canopies, jeweled and golden arches, and rows of various banners and eaves.
Resounding with the cries of peacocks, pigeons, and bees, and auspicious with the sweet songs of women in celestial chariots;
filled with the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, conchs, ānakas, and dundubhis, along with cymbals, lutes, drums, and flutes;
delightful with dances accompanied by musical instruments and the songs of secondary deities—[the city] surpassed all other splendors by its own radiance.
To that city of the gods, which the most unrighteous, the wicked, the malevolent toward living beings, the deceitful,
the arrogant, the lustful, and the greedy do not enter— yet which those free from these vices do enter— the commander of the army besieged it on all sides with his host.
He blew the loud-sounding conch shell given by his preceptor, thereby instilling fear in the wives of Indra.
Perceiving that supreme exertion of Bali, Maghavan,
accompanied by all the hosts of gods, spoke thus to his preceptor.

"O Blessed One, the exertion of Bali, our former enemy, is immense. I consider him irresistible; by what means has he become so empowered with splendor? No one anywhere is capable of withstanding him."
As if drinking this world with his mouth, as if licking the ten directions,
and as if burning the quarters with his eyes, he has arisen like the fire of universal destruction;
tell me the cause of this invincibility of my enemy.
"Ojas, sahas, bala, and tejas—from these comes this exertion.
Śrī-guru said:
"I know, O Maghavan, the cause of this enemy's rise."
The splendor bestowed upon his disciple by the descendants of Bhṛgu, who are exponents of the Veda,
is such that no one is capable of defeating Bali,
not even someone like you or even you yourself, with the sole exception of Lord Hari.
No one shall conquer him, for he is strengthened by the splendor of Brahman;
no one is able to stand before him, just as ordinary people cannot stand before Death (Kṛtānta).
Therefore, all of you, abandoning your dwellings, go to heaven (Triviṣṭapa).
"Go and wait for the time when the reversal of the enemy occurs;
for this [enemy], whose strength now lies in the power of the brāhmaṇas and whose prowess is currently exalted,
shall perish along with his followers through their own insult."
Having thus deliberated on their purpose with their preceptor, who perceived their true interest,
those gods, capable of assuming any form at will, abandoned heaven and departed.
Then, when the gods had vanished, Bali, the son of Virocana, [entered] the city.
Having occupied Devadhānī, he brought the three worlds under his control.
The Bhṛgus, who are affectionate toward their disciples, performed for him— a disciple who had conquered the universe and was devoted to them—
a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Then, by the power of that [gift], spreading his fame throughout the three worlds and in all directions, he shone like the lord of the stars;
and he enjoyed abundant prosperity bestowed by the twice-born and the gods.
Considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose,
the high-minded Śrī Śuka said:
"When his sons had thus perished, Aditi, the mother of the gods, at that time..."
When heaven had been seized by the Daityas, she lamented like one who was helpless.
One day, the venerable Kaśyapa came to her hermitage after a long time, having recently ceased his meditative absorption, finding it devoid of festivals and joy.
O best of the Kurus, having taken his seat and being duly honored by her, he spoke these words to his wife, whose face was downcast: "O blessed lady,
has any misfortune come upon the brahmins in this world today?"
For a householder in his home, there is nothing unwholesome regarding dharma, worldly affairs, or even death— which follows its own will—
since therein lies the union of dharma, artha, and kāma for those who are otherwise unable to achieve such integration.
Or perhaps guests who arrived have departed from your house unhonored by you, due to your attachment to your family, or even without being greeted by rising to meet them;
for in those houses where guests are not honored even with water, [the deities depart].
If they indeed depart, O blessed one, those fires— though offered oblations at the proper time— will surely become like the dwellings of jackal-kings,
for my mind will be distressed whenever I am away from you, O auspicious lady.
By worshipping him, one goes to the worlds that grant all desires, accompanied by a wife;
for the Brāhmaṇa and the sacrificial fire, O Viṣṇu, are the mouth of Him who is the self of all the gods.
Furthermore, O wise lady, are all your sons well?
"I perceive that I am unwell, O Brahmin, by the symptoms you observe in me.
Śrī Aditi said:
"May it be well with the twice-born, the cows, O Brahmin, with this dharma, and with these people."
O householder, these homes are the supreme field for the three goals of life;
the sacred fires, guests, dependents, mendicants, and those who seek alms— all these,
O Brahmin, do not suffer as long as they are under the Lord’s compassionate consideration.
"O Blessed One, what desire of mine would not be fulfilled,
since you, the presiding lord of progeny, thus proclaim the duties for my sake?
O Marīci, these creatures— born of your mind and body— are indeed composed of the qualities of goodness, passion, and ignorance."
"O Lord, you are equal toward those such as the Asuras; nevertheless, O Great Lord, you favor your devotee.
Therefore, O Lord of noble vows, consider my welfare as I worship you;
O Master, protect us who have been robbed of our prosperity and driven from our positions by our rivals."

Banished by others, I am submerged in an ocean of calamity; my sovereignty, fortune, fame, and position have been seized from me by powerful foes. O virtuous one, tell me how my children may regain those things once again.
"O most virtuous one, act with your intellect to bring about such auspiciousness.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus entreated by Aditi, Kaśyapa spoke to her as if smiling.
Oh, how great is the power of Viṣṇu’s māyā! This world is bound by affection.
Where is the material body, which is non-self, and where is the Self, which is beyond material nature?
To whom do husbands, sons, and others belong? Delusion alone is the cause.
Worship the Blessed Puruṣa Janārdana,
Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, who dwells in the heart-cave of all beings; that Hari, who is compassionate toward the distressed, will fulfill your desires.
"Devotion to the Blessed One is never fruitless, unlike other [forms of devotion]; this is my conviction.
Śrī Aditi said:
"O Brahman, by what ritual procedure shall I worship the Lord of the Universe?"
"O best of the twice-born, please instruct me on the procedure for approaching Him, so that He whose resolve is ever-true may fulfill my heart's desire;
for the Lord quickly becomes pleased with me as I languish along with my children."
Śrī Kaśyapa said:
O Blessed One, I shall relate to you that which the Lotus-born Brahmā, when questioned by me who desired offspring, spoke regarding the vow that gratifies Keśava.

During the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, for twelve days, one should observe a vow of subsisting on milk alone and worship the lotus-eyed Lord with supreme devotion. On the day of Sinīvālī, one should smear oneself with clay from a place torn open by a boar and bathe.
If one should indeed find [the body] in the stream, one should recite this mantra:
"O Goddess, you were lifted up by the Primordial Boar who desired a place for the subterranean realm (rasā);
salutations to you, destroy my sin."
Having fulfilled his personal observances, he should worship the Lord with a concentrated mind, whether in an image,
on a sacrificial mound, in the sun, in water, in fire, or even in the guru.
"Salutations to You, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Most Exalted."
Salutations to Vāsudeva, the abode of all beings and the witness; salutations to the unmanifest, the subtle, the Pradhāna, and the Puruṣa;
to the knower of the twenty-four qualities and the cause of their enumeration.
Obeisance to the two-headed, three-footed, four-horned, and thread-like one;
obeisance to the seven-handed sacrifice, whose self is the triple Veda.
Obeisance to Śiva, to Rudra, and obeisance to the wielder of the spear.
Salutations to the Lord of all sciences, the Lord of all beings;
salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, the vital breath, the self of the universe;
salutations to You whose body is the sovereignty of yoga, the cause of yoga.
Salutations to You, the primordial God; salutations to You who have become the witness.
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the seer, to Nara, and to Hari. Salutations to Him whose body is dark-green like emerald and who has attained sovereign splendor.
Obeisances to You, Keśava; obeisances to You who are clothed in yellow garments.
You are the bestower of all boons upon men, O most excellent one, O preeminent among givers of boons.
Therefore, for the sake of their ultimate welfare, the wise worship the dust of Your feet.

The gods and the Goddess Śrī followed him, as if longing for the fragrance of his two lotus feet; may the Blessed One be gracious unto me. With these mantras, preceded by the invocation, one should worship Hṛṣīkeśa.
Endowed with faith, one should worship [the Lord] with water for the feet, water for sipping, and other offerings.

Having worshipped Him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, one should bathe the All-pervading Lord with milk. Then, one should offer garments, a sacred thread, ornaments, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
One should worship with perfumes, incense, and other offerings using the twelve-syllable mantra;
and when resources permit, one should offer as *naivedya* boiled rice from the *śāli* variety prepared in milk,
along with ghee and jaggery, and then perform oblations with the root mantra.
One should give what has been offered to a devotee of Him, or one may eat it oneself.
Having given water for rinsing the mouth and having honored Him, one should offer betel leaf.
One should mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times and praise the Lord with hymns of praise.
Having performed the circumambulation, one should joyfully prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then, placing the remnants upon one's head, one should dismiss the deity. Afterwards, one should feed at least two brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa) as is appropriate.
Permitted by them, he should eat the remnants along with those honored guests; then,
remaining celibate for that night, on the first day of the following morning,
having bathed and become pure, he should remain well-composed according to the prescribed injunctions.

Having bathed [the deity] with milk, one should worship until the completion of the vow; subsisting on milk alone, one should observe this vow, intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu. As before, one should offer oblations into the fire and also feed the brāhmaṇas.
In this manner, one should perform the milk-vow for twelve days,
consisting of the worship of Hari, fire-offerings, honoring the deity, and the satiation of the twice-born,
beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the thirteenth day of the bright half.
He should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, and perform ablutions three times a day;
he should avoid improper conversation as well as various types of sensual enjoyments,
remaining non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva.

Then, on the thirteenth day, one should have the bathing ceremony of the omnipresent Lord Viṣṇu performed by those skilled in the ritual according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. One should also perform a grand worship, free from any stinginess regarding wealth.
Having prepared an oblation of cooked rice in milk for Śipiviṣṭa Viṣṇu,
one should worship Puruṣa with that hymn while remaining well-composed;
and one should offer an exceptionally excellent food-offering that brings satisfaction to Puruṣa.

One should satisfy the preceptor, who is endowed with knowledge, as well as the officiating priests, with garments, ornaments, and cows; know that this is the worship of Hari. O lady of pure smiles, one should feed them with excellent, wholesome food.
He should also honor other brāhmaṇas who have gathered there according to his ability; he should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and the officiating priests as is appropriate,
and he should satisfy the outcaste cooks (*aśvapāka*) who have arrived with food and other provisions.
When all— including the poor, the blind, and the wretched— have eaten,
the wise man, knowing that this is the propitiation of Viṣṇu, should eat together with his kinsmen,
accompanied by dancing, instrumental music, singing, hymns of praise, and benedictions.
One should cause the worship of the Blessed Lord to be performed daily with narrations of His stories.
This is known as the *payovrata*, the supreme means of propitiating the Supreme Person.
It was proclaimed by the Grandfather (Brahmā) and has been recounted by me to you.
And you, O highly fortunate lady, with a pure mind and self-restrained soul, worship the imperishable Keśava by means of this [practice] which has been properly performed. Indeed,
this is known as the embodiment of all sacrifices and the fulfillment of all vows.
O blessed lady, this is the very essence of austerity: charity that satisfies the Lord. These alone are the true observances (*niyamas*), and these alone are the highest restraints (*yamas*).
Austerity, charity, vows, and sacrifice—whatever it may be—by which Adhokṣaja is pleased [is the goal].
"Therefore, O blessed lady, perform this vow with self-restraint and faith;
the Blessed Lord, being well-pleased with you, will swiftly grant your boons.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been addressed thus by her husband Kaśyapa, Aditi observed this twelve-day vow with unwearied diligence,
meditating with one-pointed intellect upon the Supreme Person, the Lord.

Having restrained the wicked horses of the senses with his mind, and having taken the mind as the charioteer, he— using the intellect as the single-pointed reins— fixed his mind upon Vāsudeva, the Lord who is the self of all, and observed the vow of subsisting on milk.
O dear one, the Blessed Lord, the Primal Person, appeared before her—
clad in yellow garments, four-armed, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Beholding Him within the range of her vision, she rose up suddenly with reverence.
Overwhelmed with love, she prostrated herself on the ground like a staff;
rising up, she stood with palms joined in reverence, yet she was unable to offer praise, her eyes clouded by tears of joy.
She remained silent, her body covered in horripilation and trembling from the intense ecstasy of beholding him.
O best of the Kurus, with love and a voice faltering with emotion, the goddess Aditi praised Hari;
gazing up at Him as if drinking Him in with her eyes— Him who is the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of sacrifice, and the Lord of the universe—
the illustrious Aditi spoke.
O Lord of sacrifice, Personification of sacrifice, Acyuta, whose feet are the source of all holy waters;

O You whose fame is the very essence of sacred sites, and whose auspicious name brings blessing to the ears; today, arise for the sake of pacifying the suffering of the world that has fallen into distress!

O Lord, grant us peace; O Blessed One, you are the protector of the distressed. To the All-pervading One, the source of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, the Infinite One who has voluntarily assumed the qualities of the individual soul through His own power—[to You we offer our salutation].
Salutations to You, Hari, who are self-abiding, whose perfect consciousness is eternally augmented, and who have destroyed the darkness of the self;
[grant] supreme longevity, a desirable body, and incomparable prosperity.

O Infinite One, from You when You are satisfied come heaven, earth, and the waters; all the qualities of yoga; the three aims of life; and even absolute knowledge. What need is there to mention for human beings the blessings such as victory over enemies?
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, descendant of Bharata, having been thus praised by Aditi, the lotus-eyed Lord,
the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) of all beings, spoke as follows.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Mother of the Gods, that which has been long desired by you— namely,
for those whose prosperity has been seized by rivals and who have been driven from their own abode— is now understood.
Having utterly defeated those arrogant bulls among the Asuras in battle,
you desire to be attended by your sons— who have acquired the glory of victory through their own prowess—
after they have slain their enemies in combat, with Indra as their eldest.
Do you wish to see the women weeping in distress? Do you wish to see your sons, who once possessed abundant prosperity and had their fame and glory restored,
now established upon the heights of heaven and sporting there?
O Goddess, it is my opinion that for now those leaders of the demon hosts are generally invincible;
since they are protected by the Lord who is favorable to them and concealed by the Brahmanas, valor therein does not bring success.
Nevertheless, O Goddess, a means must be devised by me, once you have been gratified by the performance of your vow.

My worship does not deserve to be undertaken otherwise, for it is caused by the fruits corresponding to one's faith. Worshipped by you with the milk-vow for the protection of your offspring, and praised appropriately, I shall assume the state of being your son through my own portion and, presiding over the penance of Mārīca, protect your sons.
"O blessed lady, go to your husband, the sinless Prajāpati;
and while meditating upon me, who am present within your husband in this very form,
you must not reveal this to anyone else, even if you are questioned."
"O Goddess, everything is accomplished; the secret of the gods is well-guarded.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Having obtained from her lord Hari the rare gift of giving birth to him within herself,
Aditi ran to her husband with supreme devotion, as if she had already accomplished all her goals.
Kaśyapa indeed perceived this through the power of his meditative concentration (*samādhi-yoga*).
Having entered his own self, Hari’s portion, whose vision was unimpeded, deposited his seed—
long accumulated through austerity— within Aditi,
O King, with a concentrated mind, just as the wind places fire within wood.
Having recognized that the eternal Lord, the womb of Aditi, was established therein, Hiraṇyagarbha praised Him with secret names. Śrī Brahmā said:
Victory to You, O Urukāya, Blessed One, O Urukrama! Homage be unto You!
Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman; homage again and again to Him who possesses the three qualities.
Homage to You, the son of Pṛśni, the womb of the Vedas, the Creator.

To Viṣṇu—Trinābha, Tripṛṣṭha, and Śipiviṣṭa—you are the beginning, the end, and the middle of the universe; you are that Puruṣa whom they call possessed of infinite power. O Lord, you draw back the entire world as time, just as a deep current sweeps away whatever falls into it.

"You indeed are the source of all creatures, both stationary and moving, and of the lords of progeny; O God, you are the ultimate refuge for the denizens of heaven who have fallen from their celestial abodes, like a boat for those sinking in the waters.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, he whose deeds and prowess were praised by Viriñca manifested from Aditi as the source of immortality;
a four-armed person whose garments were saffron-colored, whose eyes were as long as lotuses, who held a conch, mace, lotus, and discus,
whose complexion was dark yet radiant, and whose lotus-face shone with the luster of earrings shaped like the king of fish.
Hari, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who shone with bracelets, armlets, a glittering crown, a girdle-string, and beautiful anklets,
and who was resplendent with his own glorious forest garland made resonant by swarms of bees,
entered the palace of Prajāpati, destroying its darkness with his own radiance while the Kaustubha gem rested upon his neck.
Then the quarters of the sky became serene, the reservoirs of water were tranquil, and the creatures rejoiced as the seasons were endowed with their proper qualities.
The heavens, the intermediate space, the earth, the fire-tongued serpents, the cows, the twice-born, and even the mountains were filled with joy.
At the moment of Abhijit, on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śroṇā, the Lord [appeared].
All the lunar mansions, stars, and other celestial bodies made that birth auspicious. O King, on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), the sun stood at the meridian;
that day is called Vijayā, on which they know the birth of Hari occurred.
Conch shells, kettledrums, clay drums, small drums, and horns resounded;
there arose a tumultuous roar from various musical instruments and trumpets.
Delighted, the Apsarases danced and the foremost Gandharvas sang.
The sages, gods, Manus, ancestors, and fires;
the hosts of Siddhas and Vidyādharas, along with Kimpuruṣas and Kinnaras;
the Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and the best of the Bhujagas—all offered hymns of praise.
Singing, praising him excessively, and dancing,
the followers of the gods strewed flowers over the hermitage of Aditi.
Seeing that Supreme Person, born from her own womb, Aditi was filled with joy and wonder.
Having assumed a body through his own *yogamāyā*, the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*) was struck with wonder and cried out, "Victory!
Hari, who had previously borne that unmanifest consciousness manifested as a form adorned with ornaments and weapons,
became the dwarf student (*vāmano vaṭu*) by means of that very same body, moving with divine gait even as they looked on, like an actor.
Seeing that young dwarf, the great ṛṣis were filled with joy;
placing Prajāpati at their head, they had him perform the ritual acts.
As he was being initiated, Savitṛ recited the Sāvitrī mantra for him.

Bṛhaspati gave him the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), Kaśyapa gave him the girdle (*mekhalā*), the Earth gave him the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), Soma, the lord of the forest, gave him the staff (*daṇḍa*),
his mother gave him the loincloth (*kaupīna*), and the Sky gave the umbrella to the Lord of the Universe.

Vedagarbha gave him a water-pot, and the Seven Sages gave him *kuśa* grass; O great king, Sarasvatī gave a rosary of beads to that one of imperishable soul. To him, having been initiated, the King of the Yakṣas gave a vessel.
The blessed Ambikā herself, being Satī, gave him alms.
Thus honored by that very splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*),
the young student (*vaṭu*) shone intensely in the assembly frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages, O noble one.
Having kindled the fire and performed the ritual sweeping around it,
and having strewn grass and worshipped it, the twice-born one offered oblations with fuel-sticks.
Then, hearing that Bali was performing the Aśvamedha sacrifices with great vigor, he approached him with offerings prepared by the descendants of Bhṛgu.
Carrying all the essential sacrificial materials, he proceeded along, making the earth sink under his weight at every step. On the northern bank of the Narmadā, at the place known as Bhṛgukaccha,
the Bhṛgu priests who were Bali’s officiants beheld him from afar, like the sun risen high, as they were performing that most excellent sacrifice.

O King, the officiating priests, the patron of the sacrifice, and the members of the assembly had their splendor eclipsed by the dwarf’s brilliance; they wondered, "Is this indeed the sun approaching, or perhaps the fire-god Vibhāvasu, or even Sanatkumāra, come out of a desire to witness the sacrifice?
Thus was the Blessed Lord Vāmana deliberated upon in many ways by the Bhṛgus along with their disciples.
Carrying an umbrella with its staff and a water-pot filled with water, he entered the sacrificial enclosure of the horse-sacrifice;
he was a brahmin with matted hair, a dwarf, appearing as a young student through his illusory power— Hari himself, girded with a belt of muñja grass and wearing a deerskin as an upper garment.
Seeing him enter, the descendants of Bhṛgu, along with their disciples and the sacred fires,
rose up and received him, having been overwhelmed by his splendor;
the sacrificer was delighted at the sight of him, who was handsome and pleasing to the mind.
He brought a seat for him that was proportionate to his form;
then, having greeted the Blessed One with a welcome, Bali washed the feet of the Lord,
who is delightful to those free from attachment, and worshipped them.
That wise knower of dharma placed upon his head that most auspicious water for washing the Lord’s feet, which removes the impurities of birth;
it was the very water that the God of gods, Giriśa, who bears the moon upon his crest, had worn on his own head with supreme devotion.
Śrī Bali said:
"Welcome to you; salutations unto you, O Brahmin! What may we do for you?
I consider you to be the very embodiment of the ascetic power of the brahmin-sages, appearing here in a noble form.
Today our ancestors are satisfied; today our lineage has been purified."

Today this sacrifice has been well-offered, since you have come to our home. O son of a twice-born, today my sacred fires have been properly fed with oblations by the water used for washing your feet;
and oh, this earth is likewise purified by those waters and by your footsteps, which destroy all sin.

"Whatever you desire, O Vaṭu, accept that from me; I suspect you are a seeker, the son of a Brahmin. Do you wish for a cow, gold, a virtuous dwelling, delicious food and drink, or perhaps a Brahmin maiden?
Or do you wish for prosperous villages, horses, elephants, or chariots? Accept whatever is appropriate, O most worthy one."
Śrī Śuka said: Having heard these words of Virocana’s son, which were righteous, truthful, and full of merit,
the Blessed Lord was pleased and, having greeted him in return, spoke as follows.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Janadeva, these words of yours are truthful, worthy of your lineage, endowed with righteousness, and conducive to fame;
for you have the Bhṛgus as your authority in matters concerning the hereafter, as well as your grandfather, the elder of the clan, who is profoundly tranquil."
Indeed, in this lineage there has never been a man lacking in courage or one who is miserly; nor has there been anyone who, having promised something to a twice-born, failed to give it.
O King, there are no men in this family who turn their backs on those seeking help at sacred fords or in battle, nor any who are devoid of spirit when challenged by supplicants.
In your lineage, Prahlāda shines with the stainless luster of glory like the moon in the sky;
for when he was born, Hiraṇyākṣa, wandering alone over this earth armed with a mace, found no rival hero during his conquest of the quarters.

Having defeated him with great difficulty when he had arrived for the sake of lifting the earth, Viṣṇu considered himself the victor only by repeatedly reflecting upon that man's immense prowess. Long ago, his brother Hiraṇyakaśipu heard of that slaying.
Enraged, he went to the abode of Hari to slay the killer of his brother.
Seeing him approaching with trident in hand like Death himself,
Viṣṇu— the knower of time and the best among those skilled in illusion— reflected upon the matter.
"Wherever I go, there he follows me, just as death follows all living beings;
therefore, I shall enter the heart of this one who looks away from the truth.
Having thus resolved, O Lord of the Asuras, he entered the body of his enemy as the latter was charging forward.
With his subtle body concealed by the breath of his own exhalation, his mind agitated, he felt his way toward that dwelling;
finding it empty and seeing no one there,
the hero, searching for Viṣṇu, roared in anger at the earth, the heavens, the quarters, the sky, the caves, and the oceans, yet he did not see him.
"Not seeing him," he said, "I have searched this entire world;
surely the killer of my brother has departed, for that man does not return. Such is the persistence of enmity among embodied beings here until death."
Anger arises from ignorance and is nourished by egoism;
yet your father Prahlāda, knowing this and being affectionate toward the twice-born,
gave his own life to the gods who appeared in the guise of brahmins when they requested it.
"You have followed the duties practiced by householders, by Brāhmaṇas, by your ancestors, by heroes, and by others of exalted fame.
Therefore, O bull among the bestowers of boons, I choose from you this one small boon: the earth."
"O Lord of Daityas, three steps equal to my own three steps [are yours].
O King, I desire nothing else from you than that you be a generous giver to the Lord of the Universe. Indeed, a wise man who accepts only as much as is required does not incur sin."
Śrī Bali said:
"O scion of the Brahmanas, your words are indeed approved by the elders;
yet you are but a child with the intellect of a fool, lacking wisdom regarding your own true interest."
Having propitiated me, the sole Lord of the worlds, with his words,
that man who— being devoid of intelligence— chooses three steps from me, the giver of land, does not deserve to approach me again to make a request.
"Therefore, O Vaṭu, accept from me as much land as you desire for your livelihood.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O one who has not conquered his senses, however many objects of sense there may be in the three worlds that are most dear to you—"
O King, all of them together are unable to fill [the space] with three steps; being unsatisfied even with that,
he is not filled even by the continent consisting of nine regions, due to his desire for the seven excellent continents.
We have heard that kings such as the sons of Vainya and Gaya, who were lords of the seven continents,
did not reach the end of their thirst despite their wealth and sensual pleasures;
therefore, one should live happily, content with whatever comes by chance.

A person whose self is unsubdued is not satisfied even by the three worlds acquired through effort; this lack of contentment regarding wealth and pleasure is the cause of worldly existence (saṃsṛti). Contentment with whatever comes by chance is said to lead to liberation.

The splendor of a brāhmaṇa who is satisfied with whatever comes by chance increases; it is extinguished by dissatisfaction, like a fire by hypocrisy. Therefore, I choose only these three boons from you, the best of givers of boons.
"By this much alone I am satisfied; wealth is only as much as is needed.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed, he laughed and said, "Please accept what you desire."
To give the earth to Vāmana, he took up a vessel of water. Knowing that Viṣṇu intended to bestow the earth upon Him, Uśanas, the lord of the Asuras and the best among the wise, spoke to his disciple.
Śrī Śukra said:
O son of Virocana, this is the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu himself,
born from Aditi and Kaśyapa as the accomplisher of the purpose of the gods.
"That which was promised by you to him while you were unaware of the harm—it was not well done;
I consider this a great misfortune that has come upon the Daityas.
This [promise] will destroy your station, sovereignty, fortune, splendor, fame, and sacred learning."
Hari, appearing as a deceptive young brahmin, will snatch it away and give it to Śakra.
Viṣṇu, whose body is the universe, will stride across these worlds with three steps. Having given away everything to Viṣṇu, O fool, how will you survive?
The Lord stepped with one foot upon the earth and with the second upon heaven;
since his third step was the vast sky, where could it have gone?
I consider your end to be in hell, for you did not fulfill what you had promised.
Since you are not the master over what was promised, you cannot fulfill it; they do not praise that gift by which one's livelihood is ruined,
for in this world, charity, sacrifice, austerity, and ritual action belong only to one who possesses a means of subsistence.
By dividing his wealth into five parts— for dharma, for fame, for profit, for pleasure, and for his kin— one rejoices both in this world and in the next.
O best of asuras, hear from me what has been sung by the Bahvṛcas regarding this very point:
That which is uttered as "Om" is truth, while that which is said as "no" is indeed falsehood.
One should know that truth is the flower and fruit of the tree of the self; it is sung that if the tree were not alive, that [fruit] would not exist, for falsehood is the root of the self.
Just as a tree that has been uprooted withers and falls away before long, so too the self whose falsehood has perished immediately withers; of this there is no doubt.
That which is beyond the objects of perception, void, or incomplete—that is the Imperishable, denoted by the syllable *Om*.

Whatever a man may say with "Om," by that he is surely depleted; even for a mendicant who says "Om" to everything, he is not sufficient for his own desires. Furthermore, this internal fullness consists of that which is the word "no," which is untruth.

"He who says 'not at all' to everything speaks a lie; he is of ill-repute even while breathing, let alone when dead. However, in jest, at a wedding, for the sake of livelihood, in a life-threatening crisis, or for the sake of cows and Brahmins—even in such cases of violence—lying is not considered contemptible."
Śrī Śuka said: O King,
having been thus addressed by his family preceptor, Bali, the master of the household,
remained silent for a moment and then spoke attentively to his guru.
Śrī Bali said:
What has been spoken by Your Lordship is true; this is indeed the dharma for householders, which at no time obstructs one's material prosperity, desire, fame, or livelihood.
"And how could I, out of greed for wealth, refuse a twice-born man—
having first promised, 'I shall give'— just like a gambler,
O son of Prahrāda? For there is no unrighteousness greater than falsehood," so he spoke, O Earth.
I consider myself capable of enduring everything except for a man who is devoted to falsehood;
I do not fear hell, nor the ocean of misery born of misfortune, nor falling from my station, nor death, as much as I fear the deception of a brāhmaṇa.
Whatever wealth and such a person leaves behind in this world upon passing away— for what purpose would a brāhmaṇa not be satisfied with that renunciation? Indeed,
saintly persons perform what is beneficial for all beings even at the cost of their own lives, which are so difficult to give up.

O Brahmin, who can even conceive of the various forms assumed by Dadhyañc, Śibi, and others, through which this earth was enjoyed by those irrepressible lords of the Daityas? Time has swallowed their worlds, but not their fame on earth.
O brahmin-sage, those who do not retreat and give up their bodies in battle are easily found;
however, those who, out of faith, give away their wealth when a worthy recipient arrives at a sacred ford are not so common.
For a wise and compassionate person, it is a blessing that they encounter misfortune by bringing about the fulfillment of the desires of those who seek help.
How much more so, then, for those like you who know Brahman? Therefore, I shall grant this boy his desire.
You, who are experts in the injunctions of the Vedas, respectfully perform sacrifices with rituals for Him;
let that very Viṣṇu, the giver of boons, be the supreme authority—or else, O sage, I myself shall give this earth to him as he desires.

"Even if he were to bind me, who am sinless, through unrighteousness, I shall still not harm this enemy, for he is the very embodiment of Brahman and is filled with fear. Moreover, this Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka) does not wish to abandon his own glory."
"Having killed him in battle, one should seize her; or else he shall lie down, slain by me.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus [the teacher spoke] to his disciple, who was devoid of faith and disobedient to his instructions.
Sent by fate, the ignorant man— conceited in his own scholarship, arrogant, and firm in his conviction— cursed the high-minded Satyasandha, saying: "Because you have disregarded us,
you who have transgressed my command, you shall before long fall from your prosperity."
Thus cursed by his own guru, the great king did not waver from the truth;
having honored Vāmana with water and other offerings, he gave him the earth.
Then Vindhyāvalī, Jālakamālinī, arrived as his wife.
The sacrificer himself joyfully brought a golden pitcher filled with water for washing and, having washed His glorious pair of feet,
placed that all-purifying water upon his own head.

Then all the hosts of gods in heaven— the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas— praising that deed of the lord of the Asuras with such straightforwardness, joyfully showered him with rains of flowers;
thousands of kettledrums resounded repeatedly, and the Gandharvas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and Kinnaras sang.
Knowing that this high-minded one had performed a most difficult feat in giving the three worlds to his enemy,
the wonderful form of Vāmana— the infinite Hari, composed of the three qualities— began to expand, encompassing the earth,
the sky, the directions, the heavens, the subterranean realms, the oceans, as well as animals, humans, gods, and sages.

On the body of that Lord of great opulence, Bali saw this entire universe composed of the three qualities, together with the elements, senses, objects, the internal seat (the mind), and the individual soul, along with the officiating priests, the preceptor, and the assembly members.
Then, on the sole of His foot he beheld the netherworlds, and on His two feet the earth; and on the shanks of the Supreme Person, the mountains.

Indrasena beheld the feathered birds upon the knees of the Universal Form, the host of Maruts upon His thighs; he saw Sandhyā in the garment of the All-pervading Lord, the Prajāpatis—the foremost of His own progeny—upon His private parts;
the sky at His navel, the seven oceans in His belly, and the garland of stars upon the chest of the Wide-striding One.
O dear one, he placed Dharma upon the chest of Murāri, Ṛta and Satya upon his two breasts, the Moon in his mind,
Śrī with her lotus-hands upon his chest, and the Sāman chants along with all the letter *ra* upon his neck;
the gods headed by Indra upon his arms, the quarters of space upon his two ears, and the heavens upon his head.
In the hair [of the Supreme Person] he placed the clouds; in the nostrils, the wind; in the eyes, the sun; and in the mouth, fire.
In the speech, he placed the Vedic meters; in the sense of taste, the lord of waters (Varuṇa); in the eyebrows, Yama and Brahmā;
and in the eyelashes, day and night. In the forehead of that Supreme Person, he placed anger, and in the lower lip, greed.
O King, he placed desire in his touch, water in his semen, unrighteousness in his back, and sacrifice in his strides;

death in his shadows, illusion in his laughter, and the various species of medicinal herbs in his body hairs; rivers in his veins, stones in his nails, the unborn Brahmā in his intellect, and the hosts of gods and sages in his other faculties.
The hero beheld all beings, both stationary and moving, within his vital breaths and his limbs; O dear one, seeing this entire world within the Self of All, all the asuras were overcome with despair,
[beholding] the Sudarśana discus of unbearable splendor and the Śārṅga bow with the roar of thunder.
The conch Pāñcajanya, which has the sound of rain-clouds; the powerful mace Kaumodakī belonging to Viṣṇu;

the sword Vidyādhara adorned with a hundred moons; and the two excellent quivers containing inexhaustible arrows—these, along with the chief attendants headed by Sunanda and the guardians of the worlds, waited upon the Lord.

O King, the Lord of Great Strides shone forth, adorned with a shimmering crown, armlets, fish-shaped earrings, the Śrīvatsa mark, the finest jewel, a girdle, and garments; He was encircled by a swarm of bees, a garland, and a forest-wreath.
With one foot He traversed the earth of Bali, the sky with His body, and the directions with His arms.
The second step of Urukrama reached the third heaven, yet not even an atom of it remained for the third; his foot then ascended higher and higher, passing beyond Maharloka, Janaloka, and Tapas.
Śrī Śuka said:
Perceiving the truth, the lotus-born Brahmā approached him, his own splendor eclipsed by the moon-like luster of [Kṛṣṇa’s] nails;
likewise arrived the sages headed by Marīci, those of great vows such as Sanandana and other yogis, O King,
as well as the Vedas and Upavedas, the observances (niyamas) along with the restraints (yamas), and the systems of logic, history, the Vedāṅgas, the Purāṇas, and the Saṃhitās.

And others, whose karmic impurities were burnt away by the fire of knowledge kindled by the wind of yoga, offered their salutations; through the power of remembering Him, they attained the unborn abode of Svāyambhuva.
Then, Brahmā, born from the lotus, offered water for worship to the raised foot of Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped him with devotion, the pure-eared Brahmā himself praised him, for he was born from the lotus-navel of that very Lord.

O King, the water from the water-pot of the Creator became the celestial river (the Gaṅgā) by virtue of its purity through washing the feet of the Wide-striding One; falling from the sky, she purifies the three worlds just as the glorious fame of the Blessed One does.
Brahmā and the other lords of the worlds, together with their followers, respectfully brought offerings to their own Lord, who had withdrawn his own manifested power,
with waters, honors, garlands, and divine perfumes and ointments.
With fragrant incenses and lamps, with parched grain, unbroken rice, fruits, and sprouts,
with hymns of praise and shouts of "Victory! marked by His heroic majesty,
and with dancing, instrumental music, singing, and the sounds of conchs and kettledrums.
Jāmbavān, the king of the bears, swift as thought, caused the sound of kettledrums to proclaim victory and a great festival in all directions,
having seen that the entire earth had been won through the pretext of requesting three paces of land.
The demons, filled with extreme indignation toward their master who was initiated for the sacrifice, said:
"This is not a mere Brahmin in name; he is Viṣṇu, the foremost of illusionists, disguised in the form of a twice-born, desiring to accomplish the work of the gods."
"By this enemy in the form of a young brahmin student, who is now begging,
all our possessions have been taken away from our master, who has laid down his staff upon the sacrificial grass,
who is constant in the vow of truth, and who is especially consecrated for sacrifice."
"It is not possible for one who is devoted to the brāhmaṇas and compassionate to speak untruth;
therefore, his execution and our service to our master is our duty.
Having said this, the asuras, the followers of Bali, seized their weapons.

O King, all of them, with tridents and spears in hand, rushed toward Vāmana out of anger against Bala, even though they did not wish to kill him. Seeing those sons of Diti leading their armies charging forward, O monarch—
Laughing, the attendants of Viṣṇu raised their weapons and repelled him;
they were Nanda, Sunanda, Jaya, Vijaya, Prabala, Bala,
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Viṣvaksena, and Patattrirāj.
Jayanta, Śrutadeva, Puṣpadanta, and Sātvata—
all possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants— slaughtered that army of the Asuras.
Seeing his own men being slain by the attendants of Puruṣa, Bali...
Remembering the curse of Kāvya, he restrained those who were enraged:
"O Vipracitti, O Rāhu, O Nemi, listen to my words!
Do not fight; turn back! This is not the time for us to achieve our purpose."
That Lord who is the master of all beings for the arising of their happiness and suffering—
that Supreme Person cannot be bypassed by the Daityas through human efforts; he who formerly existed for our prosperity and for the destruction of the dwellers of heaven.
That very same Blessed One exists today; however, people do not transcend time by means of strength, ministers, intelligence, fortresses, mantras, medicines, and so forth,
nor by the expedients such as conciliation (*sāma*).
"Indeed, these followers of Hari have been defeated by you many times;
yet today, aided by fate, they have conquered us in battle and are roaring at us.
We shall defeat them if fate is favorable."
"Therefore, wait for that time which will be conducive to our purpose.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard what was spoken by their lord, the leaders of the Daitya and Dānava hosts—
O King, struck by the attendants of Viṣṇu, they entered the subterranean realm (Rasātala).
Then, having understood the Lord’s intention, the son of Tārkṣya, Virāṭ,
bound Bali with the nooses of Varuṇa on the day of the Soma-pressing during the sacrifice.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in every direction throughout heaven and earth as the lord of the Asuras was being subdued by the all-powerful Viṣṇu.
To him, bound with the nooses of Varuṇa, the Blessed Vāmana spoke:
O King, O Asura, you who have lost your fortune yet possess steady wisdom and noble fame,
three paces of land were granted to me by you;
with two, the entire earth has been traversed— prepare the third.
As far as that sun shines with its rays, as far as the moon shines along with the stars, and as far as the rain-cloud pours down—so vast is this earth of yours.
By a single step of mine, the earthly realm (bhūrloka) has been traversed; by my body, the sky and the directions have been reached.
"By your second act, your own world has been seen by you through your own self;
since you did not grant what was promised, residence in hell is ordained for you. Therefore, enter hell, authorized as you are by your guru."
The desires of such a person are in vain; heaven is far from him, and he falls downward.
He who deceives a seeker by not giving what was promised—by you, who pride yourself on your wealth, I have been deceived with the words, "I shall give."
"Enjoy for some years the fruit of that offense, which is hell.
Śrī Śuka said:
"O King, having been thus treated with hostility by the Lord, the asura Bali—"
Though being tormented, his soul remained undivided, and with words that were not distressed by the provocation,
Śrī Bali said:
"O Lord of the gods, O You of excellent renown, if You consider my spoken word to be false..."
"I shall perform this truth; let it not be a deception. Place your own third foot upon my head.

I do not fear falling into hell, nor being deprived of my station, nor the binding of nooses, nor calamities difficult to overcome, nor even the hardship of poverty or your punishment; I tremble far more at the reproach of the wicked."
I consider the punishment bestowed by the most worthy to be the most praiseworthy for men—
indeed, that which neither mother, father, brother, nor friends would prescribe.
You are surely our supreme preceptor, though you remain beyond the perception of us asuras.

He who has bestowed upon us, who were blinded by manifold forms of pride, the eye that prevents our downfall; through the cultivation of attachment toward Him, even those other than the gods have attained that perfection which is achieved only by the single-minded yogis.
"By him, the performer of many deeds, I have been subdued by you and bound with the nooses of Varuṇa; yet I am neither excessively ashamed nor do I suffer distress.
My grandfather Prahlāda, who is honored by you, has proclaimed my virtuous conduct."

By your father, your enemy, you have been brought to this manifold calamity; what is the use of this body which ultimately perishes? What is the use of those who seize one's inheritance and are called kinsmen, yet are actually thieves?
What is the use of a wife, who is a cause for the cycle of rebirth, or of houses, which here only waste away a mortal’s life?

O best of beings, having thus resolved, the great Grandfather, possessed of unfathomable wisdom, being afraid of the destruction of his own side by you, sought refuge in your lotus feet— the eternal abode free from all fear.
And now, O enemy of my very self, I too have been brought before you by fate, forcibly stripped of my prosperity.
"This life, which stands on the very threshold of Death, is impermanent; yet one of steady mind does not perceive this.
Śrī Śuka said:
While he was speaking thus, Prahlāda, the beloved of the Blessed Lord, [arrived].
O best of the Kurus, he arrived like the risen lord of the full moon.
Indrasena beheld his own grandfather, resplendent with glory, with eyes as long as lotus petals,
tall in stature, clad in saffron garments, possessing the luster of collyrium, with long arms, a beautiful bull among men.
To him, Bali, being restrained by the noose of Varuṇa, did not offer worship as he had done before;
with his eyes trembling with tears, he bowed his head and stood with his face cast down in shame.
There, he beheld Hari, the Lord of the virtuous, seated and attended by Sunanda and his other followers.
Approaching the ground, the high-minded one bowed his head with his crown; overwhelmed by horripilation and tears, Śrī Prahlāda said:
"By you alone was the powerful position of Indra granted, and that very same position has been taken back today; it is equally beautiful."
I consider that a great favor has indeed been bestowed upon me, since I have been caused to fall away from the goddess Śrī, who deludes even the self.
For by her, even a wise man is bewildered; therefore, who can discern the true course of the Self? To Him, the Lord of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, the witness of all worlds, I offer my obeisances.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, while Prahlāda was listening with palms joined in reverence,
the blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha spoke to Madhusūdana.
O King, seeing her husband bound, his virtuous wife, overwhelmed with fear, bowed down to Upendra with palms joined in reverence; with her face cast downward, she spoke.
Śrī Vindhyāvalī said:
This triple world was created by You for Your own sport; yet, O Lord, those of dull intellect would claim ownership over it as if they were other masters.
What can these shameless ones bring to You, the Creator and Sovereign, who have cast aside their sense of modesty and stripped away the doctrine that You are the author?
Śrī Brahmā said:
"O Creator of beings, Lord of beings, God of gods, who pervades the universe!
Release this man, whose entire wealth has been taken; he does not deserve punishment.
By him, all the earthly realms you have earned through your own actions have been offered to you."
And having offered all his possessions with an undisturbed mind at the feet of Him whose intellect is free from deceit,
he performed the perfect worship by offering water and even blades of *dūrvā* grass.
Even he who has bestowed the three worlds upon others attains the supreme goal;
how could one whose mind is undaunted fall into distress?
The Blessed Lord said:
O Brahman, I withdraw that grace which I bestow upon one who,
intoxicated by me, becomes arrogant and disregards both the world and Me.
Whenever the individual soul, wandering through the cycle of existence due to its own past actions, [attains such a state].
This powerless being may attain the human state after passing through various wombs; yet if he should not become arrogant because of his birth,
actions, age, form, learning, power, wealth, and so forth,
then that is my grace upon him.
Alas, one who is devoted to Me should not become deluded by birth and other conditions arising from pride and arrogance, which on all sides oppose every form of ultimate well-being;
for this leader of the Dānavas and Daityas is a promoter of fame.
He conquered the unconquerable Māyā; even while suffering, he was not deluded.
Though his wealth was exhausted, fallen from his position, cast out, bound by enemies, abandoned by his kinsmen, and made to undergo agonizing torments—
Though rebuked and cursed by his guru, he of noble vows did not abandon the truth.
"Even when told by me through deceptions that this was not dharma, he who speaks the truth did not forsake it.
He has been brought by me to a place difficult even for the immortals to attain.
During the interval of Sāvarṇi Manu, he shall become Indra, taking refuge in me;
meanwhile, let him dwell in Sutala, which was fashioned by Viśvakarman— a realm where mental anxieties, physical ailments, fatigue, drowsiness, and defeat do not exist.
"No calamities shall befall those who dwell here by my glance,
O Indrasena, great king; go now, may it be well with you,
surrounded by your kinsmen to the realm of Sutala, which is sought after even by the inhabitants of heaven."

The lords of the worlds shall not overcome you, much less others; my discus will slay those Daityas who transgress your commands. I shall protect you from all sides, along with your followers and your retinue.

O hero, you shall see me there, ever present; however, due to your association with the Dānavas and Daityas, your disposition has become demonic. But upon seeing my majesty, that [disposition] will immediately be blunted and perish.
Śrī Śuka said:
When the Ancient Person had spoken thus, the high-minded one, esteemed by all saintly persons,
with palms joined in reverence, his eyes clouded by a stream of tears, and overwhelmed with devotion, spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Śrī Bali said:
Oh, how wonderful! This effort made for the sake of prostration is perfectly focused on the task of fulfilling the purpose of surrendered devotees;
for this grace of yours, never before obtained even by the world-protectors and the immortals, has been bestowed upon me, a lowly asura.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having spoken thus and bowed down to Hari, Brahmā, along with Bhava, then departed;
and Bali, being liberated, entered Sutala joyfully together with the asuras.
Thus the Blessed One, having restored heaven to Indra and fulfilled the desire of Aditi, governed the entire world; and he bestowed upon Bali,
who had received his grace and was released, his grandson as the upholder of his lineage.
Having heard this, Prahlāda, his heart inclined toward devotion, spoke as follows.
Śrī Prahlāda said:
Neither Viriñca, nor Śrī, nor Śarva receives such grace from Him, much less others.

O protector of our fortress from the asuras, whose feet are saluted by those worthy of universal homage; O giver of refuge, by partaking of the nectar of whose lotus feet Brahmā and the other gods obtain their divine powers.
Why have we, who are indeed of crooked ways and born of wicked wombs, been brought by you into the path of your compassionate gaze? Oh,
how wonderful is your deed, endowed with immeasurable yogic power!

O Lord who has playfully emanated the universe, you who are all-knowing, the Self of all, and impartial; since your nature is even and you are dear to your devotees, your very essence is that of the wish-fulfilling tree.
The Blessed Lord said:
"My child Prahlāda, may you be blessed; go to your abode in Sutala, rejoicing with your grandson, and bring happiness to your kinsmen."
"There you shall constantly behold me standing with mace in hand;
by the great joy of seeing me, the bondage of your karma shall be destroyed.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, Prahlāda, whose wisdom was stainless, together with Bali, accepted the command of the Blessed One, saying "So be it," and placing his joined palms to his head,
