that commander of all the demon hosts circumambulated the Primal Person.

Having bowed down and received his permission, he entered the great cave. Then, O King, Hari Nārāyaṇa was seated nearby in the assembly of those who discourse on Brahman, in the midst of the officiating priests.
"O Brahmin, may you mend the flaw in the ritual of this disciple who is performing his duties;
may that inequality in the rites which was perceived by Brahmā become equal.
Śrī Śukra said:

Whence could there be such inequality of karma for one whose master of karma you are, O Lord of sacrifice, Person of sacrifice, who has been worshipped with his whole being? [Yet] there may be a deficiency in the mantra, the ritual procedure, or in the place, time, and materials.
O Infinite One, although the constant chanting of Your names makes everything perfect and flawless,
nevertheless, as You speak, I shall follow Your instruction; for the highest good for men is the observance of Your command.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus accepted the command of Hari, the venerable Uśanas,
together with the brahmin-sages, rectified the deficiencies in Bali’s sacrifice.
O King, having thus begged the earth from Bali, Hari, the dwarf,
gave back to his brother Mahendra the celestial realm that had been seized by his enemies.
Brahmā, the Lord of the Prajāpatis, was then honored by the gods, sages, ancestors, and kings.
At the request of Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and other leaders, as well as Kumāra and Bhava,
for the pleasure of Kaśyapa and Aditi, and for the welfare of all beings,
he made Vāmana the lord of the worlds and the world-protectors.
For the sake of the prosperity of all the Vedas, all the gods, dharma, fame, and fortune,
as well as for the auspiciousness of vows and the attainment of heaven and liberation,
he fashioned Upendra as the Lord for the manifestation of all divine powers.
Then, O King, all living beings rejoiced exceedingly.
Thereupon Indra, placing Vāmana at the forefront, led him to heaven by way of the path of the gods,
accompanied by the world-protectors and with the approval of Brahmā.
Having regained the three worlds, O King, Indra— protected by the arms of Upendra and endowed with supreme splendor— rejoiced, his fear having vanished;
as did Brahmā, Śiva, Kumāra, and the sages headed by Bhṛgu.
The ancestors, all living beings, the perfected ones (siddhas), and those who travel in celestial chariots (vaimānikas),
singing of that most wonderful and great deed of Viṣṇu,
returned to their own abodes and praised Aditi.
O delighter of your lineage, I have related all this to you—
the life-story of the Wide-Striding One (Urukrama), which liberates listeners from sin.
I am unable to reach the further shore of the greatness of Him who strides widely.
"Which mortal has measured out the earthly particles? Does a mortal, while being born or already born, attain [immortality]?
Thus spoke the seer who perceived the mantra, concerning that Supreme Person.

He who hears this account of the incarnations of Hari, the God of gods and performer of wondrous deeds, attains the supreme goal. This [account] should be recited while performing rites for the gods, the ancestors, or those pertaining to humans.
"Wherever this [account] is recited, know that to be the meritorious deed of those [reciters].
The King said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear of the wonderful deeds of Hari."

This is the account of the first incarnation, the imitation of a fish by Māyā; for what purpose the Lord assumed that form despised by the world— like a sovereign seized by karma, though his nature is beyond the reach of darkness and impatience.
"O Blessed One, you ought to relate all of this to us exactly as it is—
the life of Uttamaśloka, which brings happiness to all the worlds.
Śrī Sūta said:
Thus addressed by Viṣṇurāta, the venerable son of Bādarāyaṇa spoke of the deeds performed by the Lord in the form of a fish. Śrī Śuka said:
The Lord, desiring the protection of cows, brāhmaṇas, demigods, and saintly persons, as well as of the Vedas, assumes various forms for the sake of dharma and artha,
moving among high and low beings like the wind.

Because it is devoid of the qualities (*guṇa*), the intellect does not undergo the state of being high or low due to those qualities. At the end of a kalpa, O King, there occurs the occasional dissolution (*naimittika-laya*) of Brahmā; therein, the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are submerged by the oceans.
When the Creator, overcome by sleep that had come upon him in due time and desiring to rest, was about to lie down, the powerful Hayagrīva snatched away from his mouth the Vedas that were emerging,
while standing nearby. Having learned of this deed of the lord of the Dānavas, Hayagrīva—
The Blessed Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, assumed the form of a small fish.
There, a certain great royal sage named Satyavrata,
who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, performed austerities while subsisting only on water.
In this great kalpa, he who was the son of Vivasvat became renowned as Śrāddhadeva when appointed by Hari to the office of Manu. Once, while he was performing water-libations at Kṛtamālā—
In the water of his joined palms, a certain small fish appeared. O descendant of Bharata, Satyavrata,
the lord of Draviḍa, released the fish from his palms along with the water back into the river.

She spoke most piteously to that king, who was himself supremely compassionate: "O lover of the distressed, O King, why do you abandon me, so wretched, while I am terrified by these predatory creatures who would devour my kin within these river waters?"

Out of affection, for the sake of showing favor to himself, he assumed the form of a fish; unaware of this, the king set his mind upon protecting the small fish. Having heard her most piteous words, that lord of the earth [acted accordingly].
Having placed her in a water-jar, the compassionate sage brought her to his hermitage.

There, however, after only one night, she grew so large that she found no room within the water-pot; thus, she spoke these words to the lord of the earth: "BhP_08.24.017/1 Sā tu tatraikarātreṇa vardhamānā kamaṇḍalau / BhP_08.24.017/3 Alabdhvātmāvakāśaṃ vai idamāha mahīpatim //"
"I do not wish to dwell here in this water-pot in such hardship;
provide me with a spacious dwelling where I may live in comfort. Taking it from him, he then placed it in the water of a wooden trough.
Thrown there, she grew three cubits in a moment.
"O King, this dwelling place is not sufficient for me to live happily;
grant me a broad space, for I have come to you for refuge."
Then, O King, having been taken up by the king and thrown into a lake,
that great fish grew by enveloping itself with its own body.
"O King, this water is not for my well-being, for I am a dweller of the waters."

"Place me in a lake that does not dry up, by means of a protective arrangement. Thus addressed, he led the fish from place to place; when it was no longer contained within those various reservoirs, he cast that great fish into the ocean.
Being cast away, he said to him: "O hero, here the crocodiles and other creatures of exceeding strength devour me; you ought not to abandon me.
Thus was he deluded by him who spoke such charming words.
He said to him: "Who are you, deluding us with this form of a fish?
We have never seen, nor even heard of, such a powerful aquatic creature as you, who has filled this lake for a hundred *yojanas* in a single day."
Surely you are the Lord himself, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable;
for the sake of favoring all beings, you have assumed this form of an aquatic creature. Salutations to you, O Supreme Person, the Lord of maintenance, creation, and dissolution.
O All-pervading Lord, You are indeed the primary refuge and the goal of our own selves for us who are Your surrendered devotees.
All Your incarnations through divine play are the causes of prosperity for all living beings. I desire to know this form which has been assumed by You.
O lotus-eyed one, for you whose self is dear to all friends, service at your feet can never be in vain;
yet, as it was with other beings who perceive you as separate from themselves, this wondrous form of yours has indeed appeared so strange to us.
Śrī Śuka said:

To King Satyavrata, who was speaking thus at the end of the yuga, the Lord of the universe, assuming the form of a fish and desiring to sport in the ocean of dissolution, spoke these pleasing words, for He is dear to those who are single-mindedly devoted to Him. The Blessed Lord said:

O subduer of enemies, on the seventh day from today, this triple world— consisting of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and the rest— will indeed be submerged in the ocean of dissolution. At that time, when the three worlds are dissolving into the waters of the universal destruction (saṃvarta), [the Lord will remain].
"A certain large boat, sent by me, will wait for you; meanwhile,
surrounded by the seven ṛṣis and accompanied by all living beings, you must take all the medicinal herbs and various kinds of seeds."
Having boarded a large boat,
you shall move about undaunted upon the single ocean that is devoid of light, sustained solely by the spiritual luster of the sages; for that boat will be tossed about by a powerful wind.
"When I have arrived, bind me to your horn with the great serpent. O Lord, together with the sages and the boat,
I shall roam, dragging you through the ocean for as long as the night of Brahmā lasts."
"And you shall know my own majesty, which is designated as the Supreme Brahman,
revealed within your heart through my grace and by means of your inquiries. Having thus instructed the king, Hari vanished from sight.
He awaited that time which Hṛṣīkeśa had indicated;
having spread the *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, the royal sage sat facing the northeast,
meditating upon the feet of Hari in the form of the fish.
Then the ocean, overflowing its shores and flooding the earth on all sides,
was seen swelling with great clouds raining down.
Meditating upon the command of the Blessed One, he beheld a ship approaching.
Taking medicinal herbs and creepers, he ascended it along with the best of the Brahmins.
O King, the sages, being pleased, said to him: "Meditate upon Keśava;
He will indeed protect us from this distress and provide for our welfare."
Thus meditated upon by the king, he appeared from the great ocean as a golden fish with a single horn, measuring a million *yojanas* in length.
Having bound the boat to that horn, just as he had been instructed by Hari in the past, [the king remained there].
Satisfied by the serpent as his tether, he praised Madhusūdana.
Śrī Rājā said:
"Those whose self-awareness has been struck down by beginningless ignorance, and who are distressed by the exhaustion of saṃsāra rooted therein—"

O Supreme Teacher, you who grant liberation, may we attain you even if we approach you by mere chance. This ignorant person is bound by his own karma and strives toward action out of a desire for happiness, which only leads to misery. May he, through service to you, shake off that false-mindedness; may he pierce the knot of the heart—he is our teacher.
By service to Him, a person may cast off the impurity of the self—the darkness—just as fire consumes the tears of Rudra;

he regains his own true nature. May that immutable one become the Lord, the supreme teacher of teachers, whose grace not even a ten-thousandth part of a fraction can be attained by other gods, gurus, or men themselves.

Together they are unable to accomplish it for a man; therefore, I take refuge in You, the Lord. Just as one who possesses sight is made a leader for the blind, so too is the ignorant man the teacher for people who lack knowledge.
You are the eye of the sun, the observer of all who see; You have been chosen as our teacher by us who desire to know Your own path.
One person directs another toward an unreal state by which one enters into darkness that is difficult to transcend;
but you, O Lord, are that by which a person immediately attains unfailing, imperishable knowledge and his own true abode.
For you are the friend of all the world, its beloved Lord, its Self, its teacher, its knowledge, and the fulfillment of its desires.
Nevertheless, the world, its intellect blinded and bound by desire within the heart, does not know you who are present there.
Therefore, O Lord, I take refuge in you, the best of gods, the most excellent, for the sake of awakening;
with words that are lamps of meaning, O Blessed One, sever the knots of the heart and reveal your own abode.
Śrī Śuka said:
To the king who had spoken thus, the Blessed One, the primordial Person,
appearing in the form of a fish and sporting in the great ocean, declared the truth.

Together with the sages, he heard the divine Purāṇa-saṃhitā, which contains the practices of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, as well as the entire secret of the self of the royal sage Satyavrata— the reality of the Self free from all doubt.
Seated upon the boat, the Blessed One spoke the eternal Brahman to the Creator (Brahmā),
who had arisen once the calamity of the dissolution had passed;
and Hari, having slain the demon Hayagrīva, recovered the Vedas.
But that King Satyavrata, endowed with both spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom,
became Manu Vaivasvata in this kalpa by the grace of Viṣṇu—
the illusory fish, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who appeared as the royal sage Satyavrata.
Having heard this dialogue, this great narrative, one is liberated from sin.
That man who daily glorifies this incarnation of Hari finds his intentions fulfilled and attains the supreme goal.
He who, having slain the son of Diti, recovered the collection of Vedas that had been taken away from the mouths of the Creator when his powers were dormant in the waters of dissolution,
and who declared the Brahman to those of truthful vows; [to him I bow].
I bow down to Him, the cause of all, who is the crooked fish.
